## Epic C — Owning my data (local-first)

### US-09 · Choosing where my data lives
As a privacy-conscious user, I choose Google Drive / Dropbox / GitHub / my own WebDAV server / just-this-browser, from a neutral picker with no dark patterns, and can switch later without losing anything (data copies down, tokens dropped, new provider lifted).

**Positioning (constitution, 2026-08-14):** cloud sync is the **durability upgrade for the motivated**, not the front door — the funnel says typed captures outnumber cloud connects ~10:1 (US-23). The picker and its place in the flow stay exactly as they are (Brad's call, 2026-08-14); what changes is expectations: US-23, not this story, is how the mass avatar gets longitudinal value.
- AC1: OAuth (Drive/Dropbox) via PKCE redirect; GitHub/WebDAV via pasted credentials validated before commit.
- AC2: Switching providers copies current data to device first. "Log off this device" clears the browser's local health copy, signs out of the active cloud and forgets the remembered backend. It does not delete the remote record. This matches the existing picker copy and log-off teardown tests; it corrects the former sentence that said the local copy stayed intact.
- AC2c: After log-off begins, late roadmap writes from that page cannot recreate the cleared on-device health copy. The page-lifetime barrier closes before the first await and is checked at the local adapter's synchronous write boundary. Successful cloud writes and offline fallback before log-off keep their existing behavior. Every other tab on the device whose roadmap backend is a cloud latches the same barrier: log-off sets and at once removes a content-free signal key (`health_roadmap_log_off_signal`), which reaches the other tabs as `storage` events and leaves nothing behind (adversary R2). Log-off sends it again after the device wipe, just before the reload, so a full localStorage that dropped the first send still reaches them (Codex re-check R1). The other tabs' cloud saves are not stopped. A tab in local mode (guest, or a cloud's on-device fallback) does not latch: its device copy is its only store, and latching would silently drop its edits (adversary re-check R2). Known residual: the cross-tab latch is best-effort. A `storage` event is asynchronous, so a write already running in another tab can land before that tab latches; the reload of that tab is what clears it (adversary re-check R1). A tab running on this browser's storage alone (guest, or the on-device fallback) never latches, so if one is open its own record stays on the device after another tab logs off: there the device copy is the record, and latching would lose its edits. A failed erase-fence write (US-11 AC3b) never stops log-off: the device keys, documents included, are still cleared, the backend forgotten and the page reloaded; the failure is reported with its own Sentry tag (`op: log-off-device`, `backend: local`, no health data), apart from a failed cloud disconnect (`op: log-off`). Tests: `widget-src/standalone/logout-persistence.test.ts` (failed fence write per backend; each guard pinned by a test that fails on its removal; a second module graph standing in for another tab, with simulated `storage` events, in cloud and local mode and with the first signal write refused for quota; controlled save completion and simulated visibilitychange/beforeunload through the actual listener wiring; no real-browser navigation or real multi-tab claim).
- AC2d: Cloud log-off also clears the existing blood-test and vitals drafts and the Lp(a) check's kept answers, using the same named off-file cleanup as an erase. The forms on the page drop their draft copy too. Unrelated preferences and cloud records stay intact, including when disconnect fails. Tests: `widget-src/standalone/connect-drafts.test.tsx` (four synthetic providers and actual jsdom matrix remounts; no live-provider or browser-navigation claim).
- AC2b (2026-09-10): Connecting GitHub refuses a PUBLIC repository, and so does writing to one. `connect()` reads the repo's `private` flag and throws before `setJson(CONFIG_KEY, …)`, so a refused repo saves nothing and leaves nothing to reconnect from. A saved connection resumes with a bare `new GitHubAdapter()` and never calls `connect()`, so `write()` and `writeDocument()` — every write funnels through those two — re-read the flag once per adapter instance before the first PUT: one GET, shared by concurrent first writes, retried on the next write if it failed. The check fails closed; reads stay ungated. Accepted residual, stated: a repo flipped to public mid-session keeps writing until the next page load, which re-checks.
- AC3: On-device guest data migrates up on first connect (merge, not overwrite).
- AC6 (2026-09-09): Cloud-storage failure diagnostics retain operation/provider context but never document titles, refs, provider bodies, arbitrary exception text or request breadcrumbs. Local console diagnostics follow the same boundary. **Widened 2026-09-10 to the server's own console:** a Klaviyo failure logged the provider's response body to the Fly log, which is unscrubbed and where a Klaviyo error echoes the address that was submitted — both the subscribe and the suppress path now log the status and a fixed message only, and the body reaches ops through Sentry, where `scrubEventText` runs over it. **Widened again 2026-09-10 (night):** the Discord bot attached the author's Discord id to a dedup diagnostic and the author's tag to a persist failure, so an account name reached Sentry beside the message length. Both `extra` fields are gone; the conversation id, the age and the length stay, and they are enough to read the event. Tests: `app/lib/klaviyo.server.test.ts` for the Klaviyo logging; no test for the Discord change (the Discord module has no test file — the two fields were removed and verified by reading).
- AC7 (2026-09-10, from a ChatGPT audit of the server `beforeSend`): a health value written into free text never leaves the app in an error report. The audit fed the hook "My LDL is 3.2 mmol/L and I have diabetes": the LDL FIELD was redacted by the key scrub, but the sentence itself survived in the exception value, in an `extra.message` string and in console breadcrumb arguments. A text scrub now runs over every free-text field of an event on BOTH sides — server `instrument.server.mjs` and browser `sentry.ts`, one shared implementation (`scrubEventText`): `exception.values[].value`, `message`, `logentry`, every string under `extra`, `contexts` and `tags`, breadcrumb messages and data, and `request`. Rules, layered on the existing key scrub: a number with a unit → `[value]`; a number within 20 characters of a metric or lab name → `[value]`; an email address → `[email]`. Error class names, stack frames and filenames stay intact — they are the diagnostic. Server-side the console breadcrumb integration is off (console arguments are raw application text) and any `extra` string over 200 characters is dropped, key and all. Honest limits, stated not hidden: condition and drug words in prose are NOT scrubbed ("I have diabetes" survives) — no word list reads a sentence reliably, and a value-free condition word was judged the lesser risk against unreadable diagnostics; and a bare number with neither unit nor nearby metric name is left alone; fullwidth digits and date-shaped numbers pass through; and the 20-character window is blunt at both ends — it misses a metric name further away and can clip a neighbouring one (the `1` in "HbA1c was 42 mmol/mol; weight 96.4kg" is redacted because `weight` sits inside its window), which redacts more, never less, and is cosmetic. The unit and metric vocabularies are literals in two files (the pre-bundle `.mjs` cannot import the clinical engine), kept honest by `instrument-scrub-parity.test.ts`, which compares both implementations AND fails when `UNIT_DEFS` or `METRIC_LABELS` gains an entry the lists miss. **Amended 2026-09-10 (afternoon):** the key scrub redacts a family of credential keys, not one name at a time, so a new secret-shaped field is caught the day it appears; the metric and unit vocabularies are DERIVED from the clinical catalogue rather than retyped, so a new metric cannot be scrubbed in one implementation and missed in the other; and the parity test covers the whole pipeline, browser and server, not the vocabulary lists alone. Tests: `packages/health-core/src/instrument-scrub-parity.test.ts`, `packages/health-core/src/sentry-scrub.test.ts`, `widget-src/src/lib/sentry-pipeline-parity.test.ts` **Amended 2026-09-10 (late):** a breadcrumb's `data` is now an allow-list — `method`, the URL's origin, `status_code` — instead of a scrub run over whatever the SDK attached, so a field nobody anticipated cannot ride out inside a fetch breadcrumb: a Dropbox request whose `data` carried an `input` object or a `Dropbox-API-Arg` header keeps only the three. Tests: `packages/health-core/src/instrument-scrub-parity.test.ts`, `widget-src/src/lib/sentry-pipeline-parity.test.ts` **Amended 2026-09-10 (sixth pass):** the key list gains the families a lab report and a patient profile are actually spelled in — date of birth (`dob`, `dateOfBirth`, `date_of_birth`, `birthDate`), `gender` beside `sex`, `patientName`, and the patient identifiers `nhi` and `mrn` — plus the generic carriers a row or an extraction hangs its content on: `value`, `values`, `result`, `results`, `title`, `note`, `notes`, `summary`. No live `extra`, `tags` or `contexts` site uses any of those names for a diagnostic we read (checked across `app/` and `widget-src/`), so nothing legible is lost. And `event.request.url` is now cut to the site and the path, with the query string dropped WHOLE rather than filtered param by param, and the path itself run through the text scrub; `query_string` is deleted outright. A param allowlist could never survive the next provider: a Dropbox download names the document in `?path=`, which no list of OAuth names catches. Breadcrumbs already kept only the origin. Tests: `packages/health-core/src/instrument-scrub-parity.test.ts` (the probe payload, the Dropbox download URL), `packages/health-core/src/sentry-scrub.test.ts`, `widget-src/src/lib/sentry-pipeline-parity.test.ts` **Amended 2026-09-10 (seventh pass):** the `navigation` breadcrumb is scrubbed too. The SDK records one on every `history.replaceState`, and the OAuth return calls `replaceState` to clear the address (`widget-src/src/storage/dropbox.ts`, `drive.ts`), so the breadcrumb written just before it carries `data.from`/`data.to` = `/roadmap/?code=…&state=…` — a live authorization code. Both fields now run through `scrubUrl`: the query goes whole, an absolute address keeps its origin and scrubbed path, a relative one keeps the path alone. Browser only; the server SDK records no history breadcrumb, so `instrument-scrub.mjs` is unchanged. Accepted residual, stated rather than hidden: an attack payload carried in a query string is no longer visible in Sentry — the 2026-08-23 sentry-fix diagnosis of JAVASCRIPT-REMIX-62 read the `exitIframe` query to reach it — while the path and the exception text still are. Test: `widget-src/src/lib/sentry-scrub.test.ts` **Amended 2026-10-01 (adversarial review of the reviewer sign-in plan):** a server transaction carries no request body, Authorization header, cookie, client address or query string either. The SDK read every incoming body and attached it, with the headers, to the 20% of transactions it samples, and `beforeSend` never sees a transaction, so a consent-form password or an `/mcp` body could leave. The http integration now reads no body (`maxIncomingRequestBodySize: "none"`), and `beforeSendTransaction` runs the same `scrubServerEvent`. The SDK also copies each cookie into span data by name, so `cookie` joins the credential key family on both sides. Server side, headers are now an allowlist, like breadcrumb data: `request.headers` and every `http.request.header.*` or `http.response.header.*` span attribute keep host, user-agent, content-type, content-length and accept, and nothing else, so an Authorization header, a cookie, a Referer carrying a page's query, a forwarding IP or an unanticipated header never leaves. The client's address goes from span data too: the SDK copies the first X-Forwarded-For hop, the visitor's own address, into `http.client_ip`, so that key and the other-end names (`client.address`, `net.peer.*`, `network.peer.*`, `user.ip_address`) are dropped. A transaction repeats the request as span attributes, so the rules follow it there. On the root span a key ending in `query` (`http.query`, `url.query`) is dropped, and a URL-valued attribute (`http.target`, `http.url`, `url.full`) goes through `scrubUrl`, as `request.url` does: the query goes whole and the path is text-scrubbed. Every child span gets the breadcrumb rule (most are express middleware and database spans, where only the peer address changes; the ones that matter are outgoing calls): a URL keeps its origin, a bare path is dropped, an `http.client` description becomes the method and origin (the SDK writes the full URL there, and a path can name a document), and its data gets the key and text scrubs the root span gets. An outgoing call that outlives its request (a fire-and-forget insert after the response) arrives as a root transaction of its own, op `http.client`; it gets the same outgoing rule, and its transaction name becomes the method and origin. An incoming request's transaction name is left as the SDK sets it: in production, under react-router-serve, it is the method and a route pattern (`GET *`), and the SDK has already cut its query; a bare Node server, or `react-router dev` with a DSN, would name it, and set `http.route`, by the raw method and path, unscrubbed (a stated residual; production is `GET *` and `POST *` only, checked over 90 days). A response's Set-Cookie is dropped by the same header allowlist. The browser still sends `document.referrer` as a Referer header (a stated residual, browser side). The header allowlist and both span passes are server-only: the browser sends no transactions and keeps its header denylist. Test: `app/lib/instrument-server-transport.test.ts` (the real SDK, the production options, real requests including a Referer, an unknown header, an X-Forwarded-For, an outgoing call to a document path and one that outlives its request; each case waits for the error event and the transactions its requests produce and checks all of them; and an event processor ahead of the scrub proves the http integration reads no body at all).

A neighbouring field such as a page count is left alone. The parity sample carries those fields, so the two copies cannot drift on them. - AC13 (added by sentry-fix 2026-09-17, Sentry JAVASCRIPT-REMIX-6G/6K): a cloud record that cannot be read at load never leaves the mount empty. When the first read fails with a storage failure (`isStorageFailure`: a `StorageError` such as the provider refusing the token — a Google Drive grant without the `drive.file` scope answers every lookup 403 `insufficientPermissions` — or a Drive/Dropbox network failure, which those adapters wrap; a `SchemaTooNewError`; a `RecordShapeError`), the session runs on the device copy instead of rejecting before `createRoot`: Drive gets the existing "signed out / Reconnect" control, the other providers the guest view with the remembered choice kept (**superseded by AC14, 2026-09-18: every provider is now NAMED with a Retry, and no fallback session shows the guest view**), and the pending-mirror marker is set so the session's edits merge up on the next good cloud session or reconnect (AC4's machinery). A defect at startup still throws, and so does a bare `fetch` rejection from the GitHub and WebDAV adapters (a `TypeError`, not a storage failure) — stated, not covered (**superseded by AC13b, 2026-10-20, PR #185**). The failure reaches Sentry once, scrub-shaped (`area=cloud-sync op=load backend=<provider>`, fixed message; a network failure keeps the existing "Network request did not answer" wording), never with the provider's body. Before this, `main()` awaited the first read with no catch, so those users saw an empty mount on every visit until they cleared site storage. Stated residuals: the Reconnect copy says "signed out" for a grant that is alive but refusing, and for a file a newer bundle wrote; for a scope-less grant, Reconnect's popup can return the same scope-less token and drops the stored refresh token (pre-existing popup behaviour), so the user loops back here until they reconnect through the picker and grant Drive. Nothing checks the granted scope at connect time: the connect-time lift already answers 403 inside `liftLocalInto`, which swallows it by design and lets the connect count as a success — refusing there is the next fix (proposal in `docs/loops/sentry-fix/2026-09-17.md`). Tests: `widget-src/standalone/load-fallback.test.ts` (5), `widget-src/src/lib/storage-telemetry.test.ts` ("keeps the load operation").
- AC13b (2026-10-20, PR #185 by @robertaustinbell): GitHub and WebDAV record reads use the shared `fetchOrFail` transport: a rejected request or interrupted body, and a 30-second deadline where `AbortSignal.timeout` is available, select AC13's existing on-device boot fallback with the provider named and pending sync marked. The deadline includes the response body and aborts the request; browsers without that API retain the helper's existing unbounded behavior. Successful reads, 404, auth refusals, conflict and schema/corruption handling keep their existing semantics; programming errors outside the transport still throw. - AC14 (added 2026-09-18, adversarial review of PR #106; **the marker's `keepNewerThan` window superseded by AC23, 2026-10-20: rows the erase did not list survive instead**): nothing typed during a fallback session is lost when the cloud comes back. The device runs on the last local copy — usually an EMPTY file at `eraseEpoch` 0 — so a cloud record that has ever been erased outranks it, and `mergeFiles`' erase gate hands the cloud the file WHOLESALE: every measurement, lab value, supplement and document of that session went with no error and no event. The marker now records WHEN the session went on-device (`markSyncPending` stamps the first failure and never moves it forward while it stands), and both merges back up — `RoadmapStore.create()`'s mirror lift and the connect-time `liftLocalInto` — pass it as `mergeFiles(local, remote, { keepNewerThan })`. In the epoch-mismatch branch only, the device copy is PRUNED to the rows it stamped at or after that instant (one `ROW_STAMPS` table names the arrays and their stamps) on top of the winner's own file, and the two go back through the ordinary equal-epoch merge — so the rows meet the SAME slot, key and union rules as any other row, no slot ends with two active rows, and the epoch, the singletons and the clocks all stay the winner's. `profile`, `screenings` and `reminderOptIn` are last-write-wins singletons a stale device clock could resurrect, and `recommendationSnapshots` carries no stamp to judge by, so none of them travel: a fallback edit to the profile or the screening answers is still lost to the gate — stated, not covered. Second half of the same review: every cloud provider now gets the reconnect state, not Drive alone. Dropbox, GitHub and WebDAV used to fall back into the GUEST "choose where to save" view, which invites a user who has already placed their record to pick a second provider and orphan the first; the plan panel now says "<Provider> could not be reached", offers Retry and "Use this browser only", and the picker treats the unreachable provider as the current one — `prepareSwitch` refuses to leave a cloud it could not copy down instead of switching silently, and the copy-down it runs carries the marker too, so an erased cloud file coming DOWN cannot wipe the rows the fallback session is still holding. The marker stamps the last moment device and cloud were in step — the store's last successful load or save, and for a failed first lift the oldest row on the device — not the moment the failure surfaced, or a row typed during the debounce would be read as stale. Two residuals, stated plainly: (a) rows written between that moment and a LATER erase on another device come back by design — the merge cannot tell "typed while offline" from "typed before someone erased the record", and it prefers keeping the user's typing to honouring an erase it learns about afterwards; (b) a row synced down from a device whose clock runs fast can be stamped at or after `since` and travel past a later erase for the same reason, because no row records which device wrote it. A per-file `erasedAt` (so every writer, not just the widget, keeps genuinely post-erase rows) is the deeper fix and is not built (**built 2026-10-20 as AC20; the marker still speaks beside it, for the device copy, and keeps every stamped array**). Tests: `merge.test.ts` (8, `keepNewerThan`: the kept/dropped split, the exact-instant row, the clock guard, the stale-profile guard and its field-stamped twin (US-10 AC6), the device-erased case, no-option), `load-fallback.test.ts` (3, the marker, a row typed before the failing save, end-to-end survival), `connect-migrate.test.ts` (1, the erased copy-down), `connect.test.ts` (3, `prepareSwitch`), `storage-copy.test.tsx` (1, the retry state).

- AC16 (added by sentry-fix 2026-09-24, Sentry JAVASCRIPT-REMIX-6T, with 6N and 6J): a browser that blocks site storage still gets the widget. `main()` awaits the backend choice before the mount is rendered, and that choice read the remembered provider from `localStorage` bare, so every shape the field reported — the global missing (Safari 26.6 on a Mac, "Can't find variable"), the getter throwing a SecurityError (Chrome Mobile on Android, "Access is denied"), the property being `null` (an old Android WebView) — rejected before `createRoot` and the user saw an empty mount on every visit. - **Accepted residuals, stated 2026-09-10 (late).** (1) Shopify signs the QUERY STRING of an app-proxy request and nothing else, so a captured signed URL can be replayed with any POST body for the ten minutes its timestamp allows. What bounds it is the per-IP and per-visitor limiters on the routes behind it, not the signature. (2) The Resend webhook carries no replay nonce. Its handler is idempotent — it suppresses and deletes by email address — so a replayed delivery event reaches the same end state, and a per-machine seen-set would be partial anyway: the two Fly apps do not share memory. Both are written down rather than fixed.
- **Decided 2026-09-10: upgrade react-router 7.17.0 → 7.18.3.** Three published advisories applied to the version we pinned: a route-matching denial of service, a `deserializeErrors` issue that lands on admin-page hydration, and a client-side open redirect. Taken rather than deferred. `react-router`, `@react-router/dev`, `@react-router/serve`, `@react-router/node` and `@react-router/fs-routes` all move to `^7.18.3` (`@react-router/express` follows as a transitive of `serve`); the only other lockfile change is three dev-tool entries flipping from devOptional to dev, a --legacy-peer-deps artefact that drops typescript and tsx from the production image, where nothing needs them. The `dist/development` resolution workaround is still required on 7.18.3 and was re-verified — see the gotcha in `docs/reference.md`. Gates: `typecheck:server` clean, the SSR build passes the `generateBundle` guard with the production chunk inlined, `test:all` 2923 passed / 3 skipped, and `npm audit --omit=dev` drops from 9 (1 high) to 4 moderate — every react-router advisory cleared, leaving only `morgan` and `qs`/`body-parser`/`express`, all transitive of `@react-router/serve`'s express 4. Ships on a canary deploy, since it regenerates `package-lock.json`.

- AC20 (2026-10-20, Brad chose option A on issue #110; review fixes the same day; **its `erasedAt` window and marker superseded by AC23 the same day: the window survives only as AC23's legacy rule**): a measurement, lab value or document created after another device's erase survives on every writer, not only the widget's fallback path. Every `eraseEpoch` bump stamps `meta.erasedAt` (`deleteUserData` is the only bump; the CLI, stdio MCP and hosted MCP never bump the epoch). The stamp is the eraser's clock, floored 1 ms past the latest `meta.updatedAt` it has seen (the stored file it reads at erase time, and its own), so every row the eraser had seen goes even when its clock runs behind the device that wrote it. An `updatedAt` more than 24 hours past the eraser's clock is a broken clock, not a slow one, and is ignored, so a year-2099 stamp cannot push the erase past every row written after it. When two copies' epochs differ, the higher one still wins, but `mergeFiles` keeps the losing copy's measurements and lab values created (`createdAt`) and documents added (`addedAt`) at or after the winner's `erasedAt`, and runs them with the winner's file through the ordinary equal-epoch merge, so the slot rule (one active row per metric and day), the union by stable id, the sticky `entered-in-error` and the document tombstone all hold. Only those three arrays: medications, supplements, their histories and reminder preferences carry only `updatedAt`, and a stale copy bumps that on a row that predates the erase (stopping a supplement, a statin cascade), so their stamp is no proof the row was created after the erase and the losing copy's rows go, as before AC20, unless AC14's marker speaks for them (below). The rule runs for every caller, either side of the gate, with no option. Stamps compare as instants (`Date.parse`), never as strings, so an offset (`+13:00`) or a different fractional precision cannot reorder a row against the erase; a stamp that does not parse goes. The singletons (`profile`, `screenings`, `reminderOptIn`), `recommendationSnapshots` and `meta` stay the winner's, so a stale copy's profile edit is still lost to the gate; the merged `lamport` is one past both copies'. Equal epochs keep the later `erasedAt` as an instant (or the one present). `migrate` keeps an `erasedAt` only if it is a complete ISO 8601 date-time on a real calendar day that parses (date, time to at least the minute, `Z` or `±hh:mm`; `2026-02-29` and `2026-04-31` go, `2028-02-29` stays), rewritten in UTC; anything else is dropped, which reads as a legacy erase. AC14's fallback marker (`keepNewerThan`) speaks beside `erasedAt`, for the device copy only (the losing local side of `RoadmapStore.create()`'s mirror lift, the connect-time lift and the copy-down): it keeps every stamped array from the marker on (measurements, lab values, documents, medications, supplements, both histories, reminder preferences), and a row passes if either rule admits it. So a statin, an omega-3 or a weight typed during a fallback session or after a failed first lift survives an erase stamped with `erasedAt`, and so, by AC14's residual (a), does a row the session typed between the marker and the erase. Without a marker, `erasedAt` alone decides, so a pre-erase supplement a stale copy re-stamps still goes. A winner with no `erasedAt` (an erase written before this shipped) keeps none of the losing copy, as before, unless the marker speaks. Every stamp in this path is read as an instant by one parser (`stampInstant`), which reads a date-time with no zone as UTC: the gate, `migrate`'s createdAt and updatedAt clamps and its anchor, the marker's earliest row (`earliestRowStamp`) and `markSyncPending`'s keep-the-earliest. A stamp that does not parse keeps the old text order in the clamps, so a garbage stamp still cannot win a slot. Before this, the clamp compared text: a pre-erase row stamped `+13:00` sorted past the file clock, was clamped up to it, and outlived the erase. Residuals, stated, both directions, because the comparison is wall-clock across devices and no row records which device wrote it: (a) a row written on a device whose clock runs ahead, after the eraser's last read, can be stamped past `erasedAt` and outlive the erase; (b) a device whose clock runs behind the eraser's (or an eraser whose clock runs ahead) stamps a genuine post-erase row before `erasedAt`, and it is dropped. The floor narrows (a) to rows the eraser never saw; it can widen (b), by however far the fastest clock among the writes the eraser read runs ahead of the writer's. Known limit (adversary R6): re-importing the same file on a stale copy after an erase writes nothing new, because the import dedups on `sourceFileName` and `(metric, recorded_at)` against the copy's own pre-erase rows; those rows predate `erasedAt` and go at the next merge, so the value is lost and the user must import it again on a copy that has seen the erase. Usage signal: none — a data-safety invariant with no product event. Tests: `merge.test.ts` (19, `erasedAt`: the marker's union window, a failed lift's statin, omega-3 and weight with their histories, a zoneless stamp as UTC; each side of the gate, symmetry, the exact instant, legacy drop, marker outranked, equal-epoch max, a later erase, sticky `entered-in-error`, one active per day, no stale singleton, `+13:00`/`-04:00` offsets, fractional precision, the later erase across offsets, a re-stamped pre-erase supplement and medication stay gone, lamport past both), `migrate.test.ts` (3: kept in UTC, strict drops, impossible calendar days, the createdAt clamp by instant through `ROADMAP_DOC.migrate` and the gate), `connect-migrate.test.ts` (1: a failed lift's mixed-offset documents both survive), `roadmap-file.schema.test.ts` (1), `sync-manager.test.ts` (1, an offline CLI copy through `FileAdapter`), `roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts` (4 new: `deleteUserData` stamps it 1 ms past now, a stale device's post-erase write survives, a slow eraser clock still drops a row it had seen, a year-2099 `updatedAt` does not move it; 2 updated), `roadmap-store-two-tabs.test.ts` (1 reversed: a tab's edit typed after the other tab's erase now survives; 4 given a clock that moves), `load-fallback.test.ts` (2: beside `erasedAt` the marker keeps the session's pre-erase row; a failed lift after an erase keeps a medication, a supplement, a weight and both histories).
- AC23 (2026-10-20, Brad: "do it by data", replacing #146 and #161, which are closed; revised the same day after the design review, Codex R1-R2 and adversary R1-R11): an erase records WHICH rows it removed, and the merge decides by those ids, never by clocks. The record gains one top-level field, `erasedRows: { fromEpoch, ids }`. `ids` holds the root id of every row an erase removed, sorted and unique. The root id strips both suffixes a derived row adds, `#dup-…` and `#si`, so a duplicate copy or a unit conversion goes with its original. Every production writer mints row ids with `crypto.randomUUID()`, so the list holds no values, metrics, dates or names. Nothing enforces that shape, though, so an id an agent or a hand edit wrote is listed as it is. Brad accepted on 2026-10-20 that the list shows an erase happened and roughly how many rows it removed. `fromEpoch` claims that every erase from that epoch up to the file's `eraseEpoch` listed its ids. `fromEpoch = eraseEpoch + 1` claims nothing.
  - **Older readers cannot write a listed file.** A file that carries `erasedRows` is stamped `schemaVersion` 2. Bundles and CLIs from before this refuse it on load (`SchemaTooNewError`, rule 2), so they cannot shrink the list or erase without listing. An old open tab shows its existing "could not be reached" state until it reloads into the new bundle; an out-of-date CLI asks to be updated. A file never erased under this rule stays at version 1, so nothing changes for anyone else. This gate is what makes `fromEpoch`'s claim true: once a file is at version 2, every later erase is made by code that lists.
  - **What an erase records, and when it refuses.** The erase reads the WHOLE stored record before anything irreversible: before the reminders hook on Brad's server and before chat history is tombstoned (`roadmap-data.ts`). If the user chose a cloud and that read fails, including during a fallback session, the erase is refused and nothing changes. The existing alert says the provider could not be reached, and the user can try again. An erase that cannot read the record cannot list what it removes. This replaces US-11 AC7's "an unreadable record leaves this copy's epoch". It then lists the ids of every row in the stored record, in its own copy and, on a cloud, in this browser's device file: measurements, lab values, documents, medications, supplements and both histories, `entered-in-error` rows and document tombstones included. The device file holds other tabs' failed-save mirrors from this browser. The new epoch's `fromEpoch` is the one the merge of the stored and own copies would carry, by the rules below. When that merge carries no list, it is the new epoch. `erasedAt` is still stamped as before, for the legacy rule below.
  - **The merge.** Every merge, at any epoch, unions both sides' `ids`. It drops every row whose root id is listed, from every row array, before anything else. `migrate` drops listed rows on load too, so every reader agrees: the widget, `read_record`, the CLI. A listed row can never come back, whichever copy holds it, whatever its clocks say. Reminder preferences carry no id and are not listed. When epochs differ, the higher one still wins `profile`, `screenings`, `reminderOptIn`, `reminderPreferences`, `recommendationSnapshots` and `meta`, as before. A reminder preference set in a fallback session is now lost to an erased cloud; the marker used to keep it. When the losing copy's epoch is at least the winner's `fromEpoch - 1`, every erase it missed listed its ids. Its unlisted rows then go through the ordinary equal-epoch merge with the winner's file, so the slot rule, the union by id, sticky `entered-in-error` and the document tombstone all hold. A row no erase listed is one no erase saw: typed on a phone that had not heard of the erase, during a fallback session, or by a guest connecting to an erased cloud. It is kept. This replaces AC20's `erasedAt` window and AC14's marker (`keepNewerThan`).
  - **Legacy erases.** An erase written before this shipped listed nothing. When the losing copy's epoch is below the winner's `fromEpoch - 1`, the erases it missed include such an erase. The losing copy then keeps only what AC20 kept: unlisted measurements and lab values created, and documents added, at or after the winner's `erasedAt` (none without one). The marker no longer speaks for it, so a medication or supplement typed in a fallback session against a cloud erased only before this shipped is lost, as before AC14.
  - **Merging the field.** `ids` always union. At equal epochs an absent list may be its own erase at that epoch that listed nothing (an older app erased the cloud, a newer one erased a guest copy, and the copy was lifted up), so the merge keeps the ids and claims nothing: `fromEpoch = eraseEpoch + 1`. Two lists keep the larger `fromEpoch`, which claims less. `meta.erasedAt` at equal epochs: when exactly one side lists, it comes from the side without the list, since the listing erase's rows go by id and the unlisted erase's time is the one that still decides (a stale copy then keeps a row typed between the two erases); when both list or neither does, the later of the two. A list that claims nothing (`fromEpoch = eraseEpoch + 1`) counts as no list here, so a lifted copy meeting a stale copy of the guest file again keeps the unlisted erase's time (found while fixing the re-check; orchestrator fix, not re-reviewed). The erase's own `fromEpoch` comes from this same merge, so it inherits the rule. Across the gate the winner's `fromEpoch` stands. A winner with no list gives `fromEpoch = eraseEpoch + 1`, keeping the ids and claiming nothing. Under the version gate that case arises only from a file erased before this shipped. `migrate` keeps `erasedRows` only when `ids` is an array of strings and `fromEpoch` an integer from 1 to `eraseEpoch + 1`; anything else drops the whole field, which reads as a legacy erase, the stricter rule.
  - **Kept off agent surfaces.** `read_record`'s `redactRecord` removes `erasedRows` as bookkeeping (US-32 AC41). The visible-change check (`visibleContentOf`) ignores it, so a change only to the list announces nothing (US-34 AC3). `docs/health-roadmap-file.schema.json` (US-29) and `docs/agent-access.md` rule 6 document the field and the version gate.
  - **Deleted with it:** `MergeOptions.keepNewerThan` and the marker window, `SyncManager`'s `keepNewerThan`, `earliestRowStamp` and its export, `localUnsyncedSince`, `syncPendingSince`, the marker's timestamp and `lastSyncedAt`. The marker stays only as a yes/no for the "not yet saved to your cloud" notice, so `markSyncPending()` takes no argument. The mirror lift, the connect-time lift and the copy-down become plain merges.
  - **Residuals, stated.** (a) A row another device writes while the erase is in flight survives: the erase never saw it. (b) A row typed BEFORE the erase on a device that had not yet sent it survives too. The merge cannot tell typed-before from typed-after without a clock, and keeping the user's typing is the safer error. AC20's rule dropped it; `roadmap-store-two-tabs.test.ts`'s unsaved pre-erase `hdl` case flips from gone to kept. (c) A stale copy's edit to a pre-erase medication or supplement keeps that row's id, so it stays erased. The history row the edit appended has a new id and survives, so history can show a change to a medication the current list no longer has. (d) AC20's known limit still applies: re-importing the same file on a stale copy writes nothing, because the import dedups against the copy's own listed rows, which then go at the merge. Import again on a copy that has seen the erase. (e) The list grows by about 40 bytes per erased row and is never pruned. Usage signal: none, a data-safety invariant. Built 2026-10-20 (branch `worktree-agent-a81812c48fccb76a3`). Two calls the AC left open, taken the stricter way: the device file's own `erasedRows.ids` join the list too, and a device file that cannot be read lists nothing (a successful erase removes it anyway); `visibleContentOf` ignores `schemaVersion` beside `erasedRows`, since a list arriving on a version-1 copy raises it. The plan's `schemaVersion` (`planPayload`, the `get_plan` JSON) is the plan shape's version, not the record's: it stays 1, so the hosted tool list and the `get_plan` schema stay byte-identical. `get-plan.ts`'s text and HTML reports name the record's own version. Review fixes, 2026-10-20 (adversary R1-R6, Codex R1): the equal-epoch rule above; a device file that reads but is not a valid record lists nothing, and any failure after the caller's step comes back as a refusal, never a rejection that leaves the page deleting; a losing row whose id is not a string is skipped, as AC20 skipped it; the yes/no marker is stored as `9999-12-31T23:59:59.999Z`, so an older bundle in another tab that reads it as `keepNewerThan` keeps nothing extra (a `1` parsed as 2001); the erase copy (US-11) says what is kept. Re-check fixes, 2026-10-20 (Codex re-check R1, adversary re-check R1-R2): the guest-erase copy said a cloud connected afterwards was untouched, but the guest's list removes the copied-down rows from it and the higher epoch resets its profile and screening answers, so the copy now says so; `erasedAt` at equal epochs follows the rule above. Tests: `merge.test.ts` (14, the AC23 block: a listed row dropped on both sides of the gate and at equal epochs; an unlisted row on the losing side kept in all seven id-bearing arrays; a `#dup-` copy and an `#si` conversion of a listed row dropped, with `rootIdOf`; the legacy rule when `fromEpoch` leaves a gap, when the winner has no list and when the field is malformed; union, an absent list claiming nothing at equal epochs, and `fromEpoch` rules; an old-app cloud erase and a listing guest erase at one epoch keep a stale laptop's pre-erase LDL out; a losing row with a numeric id skipped, not thrown on; symmetry and lamport; no stale singleton or reminder setting, clock past the kept rows; `rowRootIds`; at one epoch a listing erase takes the unlisted erase's `erasedAt`, so a stale laptop keeps a row typed between them, in both orders; a guest erase listing a copied-down row removes it from a cloud connected later, keeps the cloud's unseen row and resets its profile and screenings), `migrate.test.ts` (3: listed rows dropped on load, a conversion included, version 2; 3 invariant cases: an erase list on a version-1 file, without ids, naming a number; the `schemaVersion 2` case became 3), `roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts` (8: lists stored, own and device-file ids, ids only; a device file of valid JSON in a bad shape lists nothing and the erase succeeds; over a stored erase at its own epoch that listed nothing, the list claims only this erase; the marker parses as a far-future instant; - AC21 (2026-10-20, from `product_events`, 2026-07-22 to 2026-10-20: 92 Google Drive starts, 48 successes, 18 refused by AC15's unticked Drive box; the refusal counter first fired 2026-09-27, so the 18 cover three weeks; week of 2026-10-12 (UTC) 13 refused of 33 starts; product-health metrics.csv W42: 12 refused of 29 Drive visitors): the picker tells the user before they leave. Under the Google Drive option, below the email note, one line in the quiet type of the other notes but darker and semibold: "On Google's screen, tick the Google Drive box. Without it we cannot save your file." It matches AC15's refusal ("tick the Google Drive box"). Only the Google Drive option carries it, and not once Drive is the connected backend: Dropbox has no optional scope. It is a `<span>` inside the option button, so the theme's `div:empty{display:none}` cannot collapse it, and it wraps with the blurb on a narrow screen (the text column is a flex column of block-level spans; real WebKit check owed). Usage signal: the weekly rate of `cloud_connect_refused` against `cloud_connect_started` for `google-drive`; the hint works if the refused share falls below W42's (about 4 in 10 Drive starts). - AC22 (2026-10-20, same evidence, read per visitor: 29 of 86 Drive visitors who started, 2026-07-22 to 2026-10-18, reached no outcome event; before 2026-09-27 a refusal sent no event either, so some of those were refusals): the provider's own Cancel or Deny button is counted, on the redirect path only. The browser's Back button and a cancelled GIS popup never return to us and stay unmeasured, so this narrows the silent starts; it does not close them. The provider returns `?error=access_denied&state=...` with no code, which `claimRedirectCode` answers with null and nothing was logged. `claimRedirectCancel` (`storage/pkce.ts`, reached by `GoogleDriveAdapter.claimCancelledRedirect` and `DropboxAdapter.claimCancelledRedirect`) is true only when this tab's own PKCE entry exists and its state matches the URL's, so a pasted or forged `?error=access_denied` counts for nothing. It consumes the entry, so a reload cannot count it twice, and strips `error`, `error_description`, `error_uri` and `state` from the URL, keeping other parameters. `resolveBackend` (`standalone/app.tsx`) then sends `cloud_connect_cancelled` with `{ provider }`, `google-drive` or `dropbox`, nothing else: the server's `EVENT_ONLY_KEYS` rejects any other key on this event. Other `error` values (`server_error`) and a return that carries a code are untouched. A cancel is the user's choice, not a defect, so it never reaches Sentry. Usage signal: this event itself. Like `cloud_connect_started`, `_success` and `_refused`, it is sent once per event name and provider per tab session (`trackProductEvent`'s sessionStorage throttle; the provider joined the key for the `cloud_connect_` family here, so a tab that cancels Dropbox and then Drive counts both), so all four count tabs, not attempts: a tab that cancels and then connects sends one start, one cancel and one success. Read the funnel per visitor (which outcomes each tab reached, and tabs with a start and no outcome at all), never as starts minus outcomes. Counting attempts instead would break the comparison with the 90-day baseline taken 2026-10-20. The provider key does shift the unit slightly from this deploy: a tab that starts Dropbox and then Drive now sends both starts (13 Dropbox and 2 GitHub starts in that baseline), so read the first week after deploy as a small break, noted in the product-health LEARNINGS. Tests: `storage/cancel-redirect.test.ts` (5: a matching Cancel counts once and strips, Dropbox, no pending flow, a forged state and the other provider's flow, other errors and a code), `app/lib/product-events.server.test.ts` (1: accepted with a provider only).
- AC24 (2026-10-20, security fix): a customer is identified only by a query Shopify signed, and the server never hands out a signed query. (1) `logged_in_customer_id` has one reader, `getCustomerId` (`app/lib/route-helpers.server.ts`), and it returns an id only when our own verifier `verifyAppProxySignature` passes. That verifier refuses a query in which any of Shopify's own params (`logged_in_customer_id`, `path_prefix`, `shop`, `signature`, `timestamp`) appears more than once. Shopify's `authenticate.public.appProxy` (`@shopify/shopify-app-react-router` 1.2.0 over `@shopify/shopify-api` 13) checked the LAST copy of a repeated key, while `searchParams.get` reads the FIRST, so the two could disagree about who is asking. Under `@shopify/shopify-api` 15 (US-48 AC4) it refuses a repeated `shop`, `signature` or `timestamp` with a 400 but comma-joins a repeated `logged_in_customer_id` and passes it when Shopify signed both copies, so the framework check still cannot vouch for the id, and the upgrade alone would make a duplicated id pass it: the upgrade never ships without this fix. The framework check still runs first whenever a request names a customer (any non-empty `logged_in_customer_id` copy, not just the first: `?logged_in_customer_id=&logged_in_customer_id=999` unsigned gets the 400, Codex R2, adversary R2), for its 400 and its admin context, so an unsigned id gets the framework's 400, never a guest answer (Codex R1). `/api/chat`'s GET with no id and no session token skips it and returns the empty guest list (US-15 AC9). A duplicated id is not logged in: `/api/chat` answers as a guest (POST/DELETE and a GET with a session token through `getAuthenticatedUser`; a GET without one returns the empty guest list after the framework check), `/api/subscription-action` answers 401, and `/api/feedback` records no customer id. (2) The app proxy maps the whole app root (`shopify.app.toml` `[app_proxy]`), so a proxied request can reach any route. `refuseAppProxyRequest` (`app/lib/local-first-route.server.ts`) answers 404, with no Location, to any request carrying `signature`. The index (`_index/route.tsx`) calls it directly. Every admin entry point calls the one wrapper `authenticateAdmin` (`app/lib/admin-shop.server.ts`), which runs it and then `authenticate.admin`; `authenticateOwnerAdmin` and `runAdminTrigger` go through it. That covers the loader and action of `/app` (`app.tsx`), its index (`app._index.tsx`), `/app/ab-testing`, the `/app/trending-test`, `/app/reminders-v2-test` and `/app/youtube-bot-summary-test` triggers, and `/auth/*` (`auth.$.tsx`). Each route needs it itself: react-router runs parent and child loaders in parallel and a child's redirect wins over a parent's 404, and a POST runs only the child's action (a first fix guarded only `/app`, its index and `/auth/*`; Codex + adversary re-check R1). No other file calls `authenticate.admin`, and a test enforces it. The index used to copy the whole query into a redirect to `/app`, and `authenticate.admin`'s bounce page copies it into its Location, `signature` included (adversary R1); either handed any visitor a freshly signed query. The admin launch (`hmac`, `host`, `shop`, `timestamp`, no `signature`) is unaffected and still lands on `/app` with its params. Not covered: `/auth/login`, whose `login()` redirect is built from `shop` alone, and routes that never redirect with the query. (3) Residual: the signature proves Shopify signed the query, not that the request came through Shopify. A caller holding a valid signed query can send it straight to `*.fly.dev` with an `X-Forwarded-For` it wrote and steer the per-IP limit bucket `getClientIp(…, 'shopify')` reads; `Fly-Client-IP` cannot be the key because behind the proxy it is Shopify's egress. Closing the signed-query leaks in (2) is the mitigation. Tests: `app/lib/local-first-route.server.hmac.test.ts` (each Shopify param duplicated, a duplicated signature, the prepended-id forgery, repeated app params still accepted), `app/lib/route-helpers.server.test.ts` (unsigned, wrongly signed and duplicated ids refused; `getAuthenticatedUser` identifies nobody from a duplicate and a single signed id still works), `app/routes/api.chat.test.ts` (a forged first id passes the framework check and is still the guest list; an unsigned id, and an unsigned empty-then-real id pair, get the framework 400; a bare GET skips the check), `app/routes/api.subscription-action.test.ts`, `app/routes/api.feedback.test.ts`, `app/routes/_index/route.test.ts`, `app/routes/admin-proxy-guard.test.ts` (a signed request to every admin loader and action gets 404 with no Location before `authenticate.admin`; the admin `hmac` launch still reaches it; no file but the wrapper calls the raw `authenticate.admin`, and every route using the wrapper is in the list), `app/lib/app-proxy.real-library.test.ts` (the real `shopifyApp` with a dummy secret: a signed request passes, unsigned, wrong-secret and tampered ones get 400, a repeated `shop`, `timestamp` or `signature` gets 400, a repeated `logged_in_customer_id` signed over both copies PASSES the library and is still refused by our verifier, `getCustomerId` and `getAuthenticatedUser`). The customer-service gateway, which re-checks the forwarded query itself, now receives one only after this check passed.
- AC25 (2026-10-21, security fix, Discord report claim 8): no route reads an unbounded request body, save the one stated below (`/app/ab-testing`, read only after admin auth). Every other route that reads one goes through one capped reader (`app/lib/capped-body.server.ts`): `cappedBody`, `parseSimpleRequestJson`, which uses it, or `cappedRequest`, which hands a library that reads the body itself a byte-identical copy. The reader streams the body and stops at the cap. A declared `Content-Length` over the cap gets 413 unread; a lower one is never believed, and a chunked body with no length is counted as it arrives. A body that crosses the cap mid-stream is cut off: the reader cancels the stream, which bounds memory, and Node then resets the connection, so the client sees a reset, not the 413. Caps are sized to the largest honest body. 64 KB (`SMALL_BODY_CAP`) for `/api/events`, `/api/ab`, `/api/feedback`, `/api/subscription-action`, `/api/measurements`, `/api/google-token`, `/api/reminders-v2` and the MCP OAuth doors: their schemas bound every field to a few KB (feedback 2,000 characters, an ID token 4,096, a reminder schedule 20 entries), and a client registration document is the largest. 256 KB for `/api/resend-webhook`: its events are a few KB, but a refusal makes Svix retry and repeated failures can disable the endpoint, so it gets headroom (orchestrator, 2026-10-21); 2 MB for `/api/chat` (doubled for margin, orchestrator 2026-10-21; no live payload was measured): the widget sends at most 20 prior turns (`MAX_HISTORY_MESSAGES`), a user turn at most 8,000 characters and a reply at most 4,096 tokens, plus a plan context of at most 24 points a metric; even in three-byte characters that comes to under 800 KB. 1 MB for `/mcp`, as before (US-32 AC17). 200 MB for `/api/lab-import-v2`, the limit its `Content-Length` check already set, now enforced on the bytes, so a lying or chunked upload can no longer pass it. The Resend webhook caps before it checks the Svix signature: anyone can reach it straight on Fly, signed or not. Shopify's webhooks (`webhooks.*`) cap at 5 MB (`WEBHOOK_BODY_CAP`) before `authenticate.webhook`, which reads the whole body ahead of its HMAC check; an orders/paid payload grows with its line items, a few KB each, so even a very large order stays well under it, and the other topics are small. `/auth/login` caps at 64 KB before `login()`, which reads the form unauthenticated. Both hand the library a fresh request with the same bytes, since the webhook HMAC covers them; the 413 carries no body. A malformed JSON body on the small routes is a 400 from the route's next check, never an exception, so its text never reaches Sentry or a log. Not covered, stated: the admin `/app/ab-testing` form, read only after `authenticateAdmin`. Residual, stated: the 200 MB lab-import cap matches the old `Content-Length` limit and was not measured against real batch sizes; if Shopify's proxy re-chunks uploads, very large batches that used to pass will now be cut off; to be verified live. Tests: `app/lib/capped-body.server.test.ts` (a body at the cap whole, a chunked body with no length, a length that lies low, a declared length over the cap refused unread, a per-route cap, a multi-byte character split across two chunks; each counts the bytes pulled), one AC25 case in each route's suite (`api.events`, `api.ab`, `api.feedback`, `api.subscription-action`, `api.measurements`, `api.reminders-v2`, `api.chat`, `api.lab-import-v2`), and `app/routes/body-cap.routes.test.ts` (the Google token exchange keeps its CORS headers on the 413; the Resend webhook never calls the signature check; each Shopify webhook route and `/auth/login` answers an oversize chunked body with an empty 413 and never calls the library, and hands it a body under the cap byte-identical, multi-byte and invalid UTF-8 included).
- AC26 (2026-10-21, security fix, Discord report claim 6): nobody holding the public anon key can run a `SECURITY DEFINER` function. Six live in `public`: `get_latest_measurement_dates`, `correct_measurement`, `add_message_credits`, `deduct_message_credit`, `handle_new_user` and `youtube_bot_cleanup_skipped`. A definer function runs with its owner's rights, and Postgres grants EXECUTE on a new function to PUBLIC, and Supabase's default privileges add `anon` and `authenticated`, so all six were callable through PostgREST `/rpc` (a live anon call to `get_latest_measurement_dates` answered 200 on 2026-10-21). (1) `anon`, `authenticated` and PUBLIC hold no EXECUTE on any of the six. (2) `service_role` keeps EXECUTE on `add_message_credits` (`webhooks.orders-paid`) and `youtube_bot_cleanup_skipped` (the YouTube bot's cron tick), the only two with callers in this repo or claude_business, both through `supabaseAdmin`. (3) `handle_new_user` keeps firing on `auth.users` inserts: Postgres checks EXECUTE on a trigger function only at `CREATE TRIGGER` (`commands/trigger.c`), never when it fires. (4) `supabase/rls-policies.sql` stays safe to paste-run in full: the revokes sit in a closing section that must stay last, because the file DROPs and re-creates `get_latest_measurement_dates`, which resets its ACL; the three old `GRANT EXECUTE ... TO authenticated` lines are deleted. (5) `youtube_bot_cleanup_skipped` has a fixed `search_path` (`public, pg_temp`, since its body names `youtube_bot_log` unqualified), in its CREATE and by `ALTER FUNCTION`. Not done, stated: the default privileges that make new functions callable by anon stay as they are (a recommendation, since the PUBLIC revoke cannot be scoped to one schema); any future definer function must be added to the closing section, which the test enforces. Tests: `tests/supabase-definer-lockdown.test.ts` (every definer function created in the file is revoked in the closing section; none is granted to anon, authenticated or PUBLIC; no function is created or dropped after that section; the two `service_role` grants; the search_path in both places). Live check after the apply: the anon call above must answer 401 with code 42501.
- AC27 (2026-10-21, security fix, split from outside PR #207 by Austin Bell; review round 1 and its re-check the same day): a Shopify customer reaches a Supabase principal only through proof our server wrote. The proof is the auth user's `app_metadata.shopify_customer_id`, which only the service role can write. Email, `user_metadata` (the account holder can edit it, and public sign-up sets it) and a bare `profiles.shopify_customer_id` are never proof. Why: live on 2026-10-21, Supabase Auth allowed public email sign-up and the `handle_new_user` trigger copied `raw_user_meta_data` into `profiles.shopify_customer_id`, so anyone holding the anon key could pre-claim a customer id that had no profile yet; and `anon` and `authenticated` held every table privilege on `profiles`, with an own-row UPDATE policy, so a session holder could rewrite their own credits or plan. No one had used either: 0 of 1,510 auth users ever signed in, 0 sessions, 0 confirmation or recovery emails sent, and all 35 links agree with their server-written `user_metadata`. (1) `createUser` writes `app_metadata` on every new link; the trigger reads `raw_app_meta_data`; `profiles` loses every default privilege and the own-row UPDATE policy, and `authenticated` keeps SELECT only (`getProfile`). (2) `getOrCreateSupabaseUser` checks the proof with `auth.admin.getUserById`, never `listUsers` (which fails live past about 300 users). It never adopts an account by email: an email another auth user holds answers as a guest, whether or not that user has a profile row. An unproven link returns null and `/api/chat` answers as a guest: never a 500, never that principal. It logs a value-free warning, a Sentry warning without the customer id and an `IDENTITY_LINK_UNPROVEN` audit row. (3) The customer-to-principal cache holds only proven links, including those the orders/paid webhook looks up. That webhook never credits an unproven link. With no linked profile yet it answers 500 so Shopify retries (credits are idempotent per order). With an unproven link it first stores a `PAID_ORDER_UNPROVEN_LINK` audit row (order id and profile id, once per order) and waits for the insert; only then does it answer 200, so the retry does not loop and silently lose the credit, and it sends a Sentry warning carrying the same two ids, so Brad can credit the pack by hand once the link is proven. If the row cannot be stored it answers 500 and Shopify retries. No webhook log names the customer. (4) `tools/backfill-shopify-link-proof.ts` copies existing links into `app_metadata`: dry run by default, counts only, `--execute` to write. It reads every auth user directly (read-only) and copies a link only when the user was created by our server (no confirmation email sent, email confirmed within 5 s of creation, as `createUser({ email_confirm: true })` leaves it), the profile and `user_metadata` agree, the user never signed in, and no other auth user, linked or not, claims that id in either metadata. The direct connection does not verify the server certificate, so it only narrows the candidates: each is read again over HTTPS (admin `getUserById` and the profile row) and every gate runs on that record; a disagreement skips it. Accepted residual (orchestrator, re-check): the duplicate-claimant gate still rests on that unverified read alone, since no HTTPS API lists every user; only someone intercepting the connection during the one-off admin run could hide a second claimant, live showed 0 duplicates, and sign-up is off first. It is idempotent. Live dry run 2026-10-21: 1,512 auth users, 35 linked, 35 to write, 35 confirmed over HTTPS, 0 skipped. (5) Production order (docs/deploy-runbook.md): (a) public sign-up off; (b) apply the trigger and profiles sections of `supabase/rls-policies.sql`; (c) backfill dry run, then `--execute`; (d) deploy; (e) once every machine of both Fly apps runs the new code, dry run again and `--execute` if `to_write` > 0, then credit any `PAID_ORDER_UNPROVEN_LINK` order by hand. Accepted (orchestrator, review round 1): a customer whose email already belongs to another account, such as one person with accounts on both stores, is a guest on the second store; before this fix the second store shared the first store's principal. Tests: `app/lib/supabase.identity.test.ts`, `app/lib/supabase.profile-grants-contract.test.ts`, `app/lib/route-helpers.server.test.ts` (an unproven link identifies nobody), `app/routes/webhooks.orders-paid.test.ts` (no profile: 500, no credit; unproven link: the audit row stored, then 200, no credit, a warning with both ids; the row not stored: 500; no customer id in any log), `tools/backfill-shopify-link-proof.test.ts` (self sign-up with a forged claim skipped; an unlinked second claimant skipped; a pg row the admin record contradicts is skipped).
