- **Incident 2026-08-14 (sentry-fix run):** `migrateLocalInto()`/`copyDownToDevice()` had silently no-oped since first commit — `adapter.read()` called without its filename, `{file}` destructured from a `{body,version}` result, `SyncManager` missing its DocumentSpec — so AC3's guest-data lift and the pre-switch copy-down never ran. No error, no Sentry event; nothing typechecks `standalone/`, so tsc never saw it. Fixed same day (commit `665395d`): transfer primitive `saveRoadmapFileInto` beside `ROADMAP_DOC`, one `liftLocalInto` policy at all three connect flows (a failed lift never blocks or mislabels a connect; always Sentry-reported), failing-first tests, tsconfig now includes `standalone/`.

- AC6b: A failed guest-data lift during cloud connection uses `recordFailure` and the browser's strict storage-error Sentry envelope. Provider prose, document names and raw causes are not captured or passed as console arguments; the closed `migrate-up` operation/provider tags remain. Expected offline failures are normalized to match the SDK's configured ignore patterns. Tests: `widget-src/standalone/connect-privacy.test.ts` (synthetic mocked HTTP and the real scrub hook; no live provider or Sentry delivery).
- AC6c (2026-10-19, follow-up to PR #160): the rest of the connect path keeps the same boundary. A failed OAuth code exchange (Dropbox or Google Drive, in `app.tsx`) goes through `reportConnectFailure`: `recordFailure`'s fixed message under `area=cloud-connect`, which the strict envelope now covers, and a fixed console line naming the provider. The unreadable device file, a failed log-off disconnect and a failed copy-down log fixed lines, without the error. The lift and the OAuth exchange also carry two closed-list tags that the envelope keeps, so a fixed message can still be read: `errorClass` (StorageError, ConflictError, SchemaTooNewError, RecordShapeError, other) and `httpStatus` (401, 403, 404, 409, 429, 4xx, 5xx, none), read only from a `StorageError`'s own status, never from the message or the body. A tag value off either list is dropped. The Drive and Dropbox adapters put the status on every error they throw beside a response, the OAuth exchange and Dropbox's token refresh included. Stated limits: Drive's refresh-path errors ("retry later", "needs to be reconnected") read `none`, because the throw comes after the refresh returns and a status kept on the adapter would race when two refreshes overlap; GitHub and WebDAV do not put a status on their error, and a network failure has none, so they read `none`; two 403s with different reasons (a missing scope, a Drive rate limit) read alike. Tests: `widget-src/standalone/connect-privacy.test.ts`, `widget-src/src/storage/adapter-http-status.test.ts`.

### US-10 · Cross-device convergence
As a user with a phone and a laptop, edits from both devices converge without conflicts: append-only arrays union, mutable scalars last-write-wins, corrections/deletions sticky, a higher `eraseEpoch` wins and the losing copy keeps only the measurements, lab values and documents it created after the erase (US-09 AC20).
- AC1: A fast edit on a fresh page load can never clobber unseen cloud data (hydration gate before first flush).
- AC2: Deleted measurements never resurrect via merge.
- AC3: Lab slots are keyed on the catalogue key at merge time (`labSlotKey`), so spelling variants converge: an upload's "Vitamin D" and an agent's `vitamin_d` on one day are one slot with one active row, not two rows the app can never reconcile.
- AC4 (added 2026-09-09): two saves that overlap in flight never drop a row, on every backend the browser can write to. Every adapter hands `SyncManager` a version from `read()` and refuses `write()` when that version has moved (`ConflictError`), so the loop re-reads, re-merges and retries. On Google Drive, which has no conditional write, the browser adapter reads `version` before the bytes and re-reads it just before the upload, as the hosted `DriveAdapter` does; the one-PATCH check-to-upload gap remains and is caught by verify-after-write, not by this check. Before this AC the browser Drive adapter returned `version: null` and ignored the expected version, and a 10/10 probe showed a stale browser save silently dropping the other writer's row.
- AC5 (added 2026-09-25): the tab-close write keeps AC4 too. A guest's tabs share one on-device record, and each tab holds its own copy in memory. `RoadmapStore.flushSync`, which runs on `beforeunload` and on `visibilitychange: hidden`, wrote that copy with no version check and no merge. So a tab that had not seen another tab's save erased it on every tab switch or close, even with nothing of its own to save, and undid an erase made in the other tab the same way. Real WebKit, 2026-09-25: tab B saved a weight of 83 and closed; tab A, which never saved, reloaded; the stored weights went from [83, 82] at rev 2 to [82] at rev 3. Now a hide or close saves only what is unsaved, on every backend. Each change counts one, and only a save that lands clears it, so a save that failed (a full disk, a dead network) stays unsaved and the next hide retries it. A tab switch with nothing unsaved costs nothing; it used to rewrite the local record, or on a cloud read, write and re-read it, a GitHub commit each time. The local tier does the save's own read-merge-write, synchronously: `LocalStorageAdapter.readSync` and `writeSync` carry `write()`'s version check, and the merge is `ROADMAP_DOC`'s, the one `SyncManager.save` runs. Then the tab takes the merge in by the step a save uses, so an erase from the other tab clears this tab's drafts (US-11 AC6) and the page is told. A refused write always falls back to the async save: a conflict with another tab's write is passing, and the async save re-reads, merges and lands it. A refusal that repeats (a newer app's record, unreadable bytes, a full disk) is reported once per kind per page load, since every later hide meets it again. `StorageAdapter.writeSync`, the unchecked write, is gone. An erase made in one tab stands: the higher `eraseEpoch` wins, so an unsaved row in the other tab goes with its pre-erase copy, as its next save would have sent it, unless it is a measurement, lab value or document created after the erase (US-09 AC20, since 2026-10-20). And an erase made in a stale tab now bumps past the stored epoch, so it beats the other tab's erase and fresh start instead of unioning with it (US-11 AC7). Residuals. The version check is best-effort across processes: localStorage has no compare-and-swap, and two tabs can both read rev N within the propagation delay; the async save has the same limit. A tab whose device file another tab's log-off or cloud erase wiped re-creates it from its own copy at its next save, on this path and the async one alike; US-34 AC6 keeps that on purpose. Since 2026-09-25 a tab takes another tab's save in as it lands (US-34 AC6), so a tab is stale only for the `storage` event's propagation, the re-read's 5-second throttle, or while an edit of its own waits to go up. The commonest loss a stale tab could meet was a merge rule, not this write: profile and screenings merged as whole objects, last write winning on lamport then `updatedAt`, so a stale tab's birth-year edit put back the height another tab saved, and so did a units toggle, since `unitSystem` is a profile field. AC6 closes that (2026-09-25): the two now merge field by field. While the demographics form holds an unsaved edit the page shows the older record (the relay hold, US-34 AC4), but the store holds the new one, and a save sends only the fields the user changed: the hold costs a stale screen, not a revert. An edit typed after another tab's erase goes with the erased copy only inside that window. Same build, real WebKit: A's unload wrote nothing and the 83 survived the reload.
- AC6 (added 2026-09-25, design approved by Brad that day): the profile and the screening answers merge field by field, so a stale copy's edit to one field never puts back its old copy of another. Before, `mergeFiles` picked each of the two singletons whole, by lamport, then `updatedAt`, then content: tab or device B saved a height of 180, stale A then changed the birth year, and the merge kept A's whole profile, height 178 included. Screening answers went the same way. Each object now carries `fieldStamps`, a `{ lamport, updatedAt }` per field, beside its own stamp. Every writer stamps only the fields it changes, one lamport past every clock the object holds (`stampFields` in `merge.ts`): the widget's profile save and units toggle, its email-capture flag, its screening save, and the connectors' `update_profile`. The merge takes each field's newer stamp, breaks a tie on the value so both sides agree, and records each winner's stamp, so the next merge reads the result the same way; the object's own stamp is the newest winning field stamp. No migration: a file written before this has no field stamps, so every field it holds carries the object's stamp. Since 2026-09-26 two such files merge field by field too, not whole object against whole object: each keeps the fields only it holds, a field both hold takes the newer object's value, and the result gains `fieldStamps`. The whole-object path made the result depend on merge order once a stamped third copy met two unstamped ones tied on both clocks (adversarial fuzz), and Codex found a second order dependence: an unstamped or stale copy's clock was read for fields it did not hold, so merging A with C before B dropped C's birth year and the other order kept it. The rule now (the orchestrator's design): each field's clock is a pure function of the one object that holds it. A present field (a null included) reads its field stamp while the object's stamp is not past the newest field stamp, and the object's own stamp otherwise; a field the object neither holds nor stamps was never written, and loses to any write, since no writer deletes a key. Per field the newer clock wins, a tie falls to the value, and the result records every winner's clock. So the merge is commutative, associative and idempotent, stamps included, pinned by a seeded property test. An older app still open somewhere (a stale tab, a cached bundle) keeps the field stamps it read and moves only the object's stamp; the merge sees the object's stamp run ahead of every field stamp and reads that write as a write to every field, the old rule, for that write alone. A hand edit under agent-access rule 13 does the same. Old readers load the new file: `migrate.ts` has always kept unknown keys, the old merge carries the stamps with their object, and `fileScreeningRows` reads only the known answers. `read_record` leaves the stamps out and `get_plan` never showed them; the widget's "did anything change" test ignores them, as it ignores the other clocks (US-34 AC3). The erase gate and `keepNewerThan` are untouched: the singletons still never travel past an erase (US-09 AC14). An object that holds no field and stamps none says nothing, and never wins (added 2026-09-25, the cleanup of this AC; since 2026-09-26 the per-field rule above, with no special case): whatever its clocks say, every field and stamp comes from the other side; of two such objects the older stamp stays. The empty record `createEmptyFile` makes for a missing file is one, stamped now. Before this rule, a tab or device that made a removed file again (`SyncManager.save`, the local tier's `flushSync`) merged it over its own copy, and where the copy's lamport was 0 or absent the fresh empty stamp won every field and emptied the profile or the screening answers. A field cleared by a stamped write still speaks, since its stamp stays. A field is cleared by writing `null`, never by removing its key (an absent key with no stamp was never written); the app writes null itself for a blank numeric screening answer, and since 2026-09-26 the published schema accepts null on every field of both objects, never on their clocks (Codex: it rejected both). The stamp invariant, kept by `stampFields` and the merge and pinned by a property test in `merge-clocks.test.ts`: the object's own stamp is at or above every field stamp, and field stamps count while it is not past the newest of them. `migrate.ts` reads a missing or mistyped `updatedAt` on either object as `""`, an unknown time, as it reads a mistyped row stamp (2026-09-26): it took the migration's own time, so an agent's profile written with no `updatedAt` beat a real edit. Clocks compare lamport, then time (since 2026-10-22 time, then lamport: AC8), with no serialising; a tie between two values still goes to the larger serialised one (50 beats 5), as it always did. Residuals, stated: a write from an older app still carries its old copy of every field of that object, until that app updates, and so does a hand edit; the same field changed on two copies keeps only the newer write, as before; and a field is one value, so `unitOverrides` merges as one map.
- AC7: Cloud-read migration omits malformed IDs from ID-bearing arrays and malformed chat turns without inventing IDs, changing retained content or weakening tombstones. Omitted entries disappear on a later save; they are not repaired in place. Tests: `migrate-row-ids.test.ts`, `chat-history-shapes.test.ts`.
- AC8 (added 2026-10-22, Brad's decision): last-write-wins picks the newest edit by clock time. The `lamport` counter only breaks a tie in time, then the old final tie-break (the content for a list row or the opt-in, the larger value for a profile or screening field). Before, the counter decided: a device offline for a while edited at t2 with a low counter, another edited at t1 with a higher one, and the older edit won and silently put back the value the newer one replaced. This covers every LWW record: medications, supplements, reminder preferences, the reminders opt-in, and each field of the profile and the screening answers. Time is read as an instant (`stampInstant`), so an offset spelling orders by when it happened; an unknown time (`""` after migrate) loses to any known one. One instant and one counter in two spellings is a tie, so it falls to the value or content tie-break, never to the spelling; which spelling is stored is the smaller string, so both merge orders write the same file. `stampInstant` rebuilds every stamp in the one form ECMAScript defines before parsing (lowercase t and z, a space, `+HHMM`, `+HH` after a space, long fractions) and reads a day the calendar lacks (2026-02-30, 2026-02-29), an hour of 24 or a leap second `:60` as no time, as it does any form outside the grammar; so V8 and the iPhone's JavaScriptCore give the same answer for every string, where before they differed on those forms. The file's own clock is an instant too: `mergeFiles` and `stampUpdatedAt` take the later `meta.updatedAt` by instant, and `migrate.ts` rewrites `meta.createdAt`/`meta.updatedAt` in UTC, as it does `erasedAt`; before, an offset-spelled `meta.updatedAt` won a string max while being the earlier instant, and on reload the clamp dragged the winning row back below a stale device's older edit (review R1, 2026-10-22). The merge stays pure (no clock read), so it stays commutative, associative and idempotent. The skew guard is the writer's, because the merge cannot tell a clock running ahead from a genuine later edit without reading `now`, and a `now`-dependent rule would let two devices pick different winners from the same inputs: every write stamps no earlier than the stamp it replaces and one counter past it (`laterStamp`, in `stampFields`, `upsertMedication`/`upsertSupplement`, `setReminderOptIn`), so the next edit made after seeing a future stamp beats it. Residuals, stated (accepted by the orchestrator 2026-10-22): a future stamp still beats a concurrent edit that never saw it, until real time passes it, and an edit made after seeing it inherits its time, so that record orders by counter until then. For the profile and the screening answers that record is the WHOLE object, not one field: `stampFields` stamps past every clock the object holds, so after one fast-clock write to any field, every later write to any field of that object carries the future time and orders by counter until real time passes it. A device whose clock runs behind loses a concurrent edit to one made earlier in real time. A mixed fleet, older clients that still order by counter beside current ones, can settle a scalar on a value that is neither the newest edit nor the highest counter, and the cloud copy can switch between values on each save until the older client updates; no rows are lost, since the change touches only which current-state value wins. Old GitHub Pages forks and local CLI or stdio MCP installs may never update. When the file's meta was hand-edited with an offset spelling, an older client's clamp writes a row back under the old meta spelling, and a mixed fleet can then hold that row twice, the second as an `id#dup-…` copy; nothing is lost. `migrate.ts` still caps every row stamp at the file's own last write. No schema bump (ios/architecture.md D10 note, 2026-10-22). Tests: `merge-newest-wins.test.ts` (13: time beats counter on every LWW record, both merge orders; an offset spelling read as an instant; a tie in time to the counter, then the old tie-break; an unknown time loses; 3,000 seeded triples of medication lists with mixed times, spellings and counters, commutative, associative, idempotent and absorbing; a future stamp loses to the next edit on a profile field, a medication and the opt-in, and still beats an edit that never saw it), the property tests in `merge-clocks.test.ts` re-run with the time-first order, and the old lamport-first cases in `merge.test.ts` turned round.
- AC9 (clearing a profile field): clearing a saved Birth Month, Birth Year or Height is a stamped `null` write, not an unchanged or never-written field. Autosave persists it, a fresh store/form load shows it blank, and a stale edit to another field cannot restore the old value. Fields absent from both the current and previous form snapshots are untouched. A later intentional value can replace the clear; erase-boundary refusals still refuse it. Automated coverage: `widget-src/src/storage/roadmap-store-profile-clear.test.ts` and `widget-src/src/components/HealthTool.profile-clear.test.tsx` (synthetic store and jsdom callers; no real-browser or live-provider verification).
- AC4a (Drive duplicate-record reconciliation; Austin Bell's PR #218, finished 2026-10-23): Both Drive adapters enumerate every page of accessible, nontrashed `health-roadmap.json` files, root and legacy-folder copies included. Reads merge the copies in memory through the existing record migration and merge rules and never mutate Drive. An incomplete search is an error, not permission to omit a copy. Among several copies, a copy this app cannot read (bad JSON, an empty file or JSON `null`, a broken shape, or a newer schema; only a 404 is a missing copy) does not block the read. A SINGLE record that is empty or JSON `null` keeps main's behaviour: it reads as no record, and a save may write over it, since it holds no data to lose. Among several copies: the other copies load, merged, and every ordinary save refuses until it is resolved, a newer-schema copy with the update-the-app message (`SchemaTooNewError`, whose hint no longer claims reads refuse), a damaged one with "saving is paused" and nothing written. "Delete all my data" still goes through (orchestrator, 2026-10-23): a write that erases past the readable copies' erase epoch goes to the oldest READABLE copy, never to an unreadable one (even when the unreadable copy is the oldest), and the adapter raises the written erase epoch past every epoch any copy showed, an unreadable copy's own `meta.eraseEpoch` included when its JSON parses (read as `migrate` reads a counter: floored, never negative, capped), so the cloud's erase never goes down; at the counter cap the erase refuses and writes nothing. Folder adoption on a write moves only the copy just written. The unreadable copy is left untouched, and the result's warning says so and that it can be deleted in Google Drive; the web shows it in the erase alert and the iPhone in its erase result. A save with a raised local epoch takes the same path, so no save ever writes an unreadable copy. Residuals: when the epoch is raised, the page's own copy holds the lower epoch until its next re-read takes the cloud's. Rows in an unreadable newer-schema copy can come back permanently once a newer app syncs it, even if the user later deletes that copy: the erase could not list rows it could not read, and under US-09 AC23 a copy one epoch behind keeps its unlisted rows (orchestrator call 2026-10-23: kept, because raising `fromEpoch` would also drop pre-erase rows that readable devices legitimately keep). Saves use the oldest provider `createdTime`, then file ID, as the physical winner; this chooses storage identity, not which health values win. The preparatory version binds the contributing file IDs and versions, and a changed discovery or contributing revision requires a bounded reread/remerge. Success requires verification of the exact physical winner, not merely an aggregate whose missing rows could survive in another copy. A first create is confirmed by its file ID, never by search, because search lags a create; each adapter remembers the copies it found or made, so a lagging search cannot make one save create twice. A copy another device created at the same moment, when search shows it, sends the save round to merge onto the winner. Other copies are retained, not trashed or deleted. The browser's live refresh (US-34 AC1) follows every copy the last read or write found, not a cached ID that may name a losing copy. The browser caches the winner's ID and starts each page load from it, so a reload inside Drive's search lag still shows the record and never creates a second one; the iPhone keeps its known copies across a token refresh. Record reads never mutate Drive: moving a pre-folder record into the app folder happens on a write. A failed write keeps its provider status, so a 401 still refreshes the iPhone's token; a 401 or 403 after a write may have landed says both, "reconnect" and "the change may have landed", never "nothing was written". Erasure uses the existing erase epoch and row-list rules across the merged view; this does not physically scrub retained duplicate bytes, and removing the erase-bearing file out of band can expose an old copy. Drive has neither atomic enumeration nor conditional writes: delayed visibility and the check-to-upload gap remain, and a later writer can overwrite an already verified save. Other named files (`chat-history.json`, uploaded documents) keep the first-match lookup: a duplicate never refuses them, and a page with a `nextPageToken` is fine. Since 2026-10-23 the web and hosted adapters ask for the oldest copy first (`orderBy=createdTime`), so with two chat copies every device reads, saves and erases the same one; the other copy's bytes stay. The browser searches on every read and keeps its cached chat ID only for a search that lags a create, so a cached newer copy does not bypass the order. The iPhone does not: its HTTP allow-list (`EngineHTTP.swift`) has no `orderBy`, so it keeps Drive's own first match until that list gains it. No schema or clinical algorithm change, and the merge itself is unchanged; the erase-policy change is the adapter's raised epoch above. Synthetic real-adapter coverage: `widget-src/src/storage/drive-first-save.test.ts` (each new case cites AC4a) and `sync-manager.test.ts` (a save cancelled after its write still says it may have landed); live-provider acceptance is not claimed: no scratch Drive credential exists on this Mac (2026-10-23).

### US-11 · Deleting my data
As a user, I can erase everything from the tool on every device (eraseEpoch bump + empty flush); there is no server copy to chase. Since US-09 AC23 the erase removes every row it can see in this browser and the connected cloud file; a value another device has not yet saved, or saves while the erase runs, is kept and arrives later; for a guest erase, "With no cloud connected, the values in this browser are erased. If you later connect a cloud, the same values are erased there too and its profile and screening answers are reset; values this browser never held stay." The confirm, the alert and the privacy addendum say so (`HealthTool.erase-copy.test.ts`).
- AC1 (2026-09-10): an erase clears the health data that sits OUTSIDE the record file, in every mode. The uploaded document blobs (`health_roadmap_doc_v2:*`) and both matrices' typed-but-unsaved drafts (`health_roadmap_bt_timeline_draft`, and `health_roadmap_vitals_draft` since 2026-09-24) go by name, and so, since 2026-10-13, do the Lp(a) check's kept answers (`health_roadmap_lpa_check_kept`, US-05 AC3), which name rows of the record. Before this, a localStorage-only user kept every document blob: the residue wipe ran only with a cloud connected, because it goes through `LocalStorageAdapter.disconnect()`, which in local mode would delete the erased file the erase had just written; and the draft survived an erase on every backend. The clear is a NAMED list, never a prefix wipe. `health_roadmap_*` also holds the cloud tokens, the remembered backend, the device id and the consent keys (`hr_reminders_autoenrol_blocked`, `hr_ab`, `hr_vid`), and taking those would log the user out and reset decisions they had already made. `hr_anthropic_key` stays as well: it is a credential the user typed, not health data. The notice now says what an erase cannot reach: the original documents already in the user's cloud folder, which no adapter deletes, and the provider's version history, GitHub keeping every past version. Tests: `widget-src/src/storage/roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts`, "RoadmapStore.deleteUserData clears off-file health data (US-11 AC1)" (3: local mode, cloud mode, and the keep-list of tokens, consent flags and the typed API key).
- AC2 (2026-09-10): an erase reaches `chat-history.json`. The record erase never touched it, so every conversation the user had ever held stayed in their cloud folder. It cannot be emptied by writing an empty file: the chat merge unions conversations by id, so any other device's copy would put them all back. So the erase TOMBSTONES every conversation instead (`deleted: true`, no messages, blank title, bumped `updatedAt`) and a tombstone is monotonic. The title is blanked because it is the user's own first sentence; the merge now drops a tombstone's title the way it already dropped its messages, so a same-millisecond tie cannot bring it back. It runs through the `getChatHistory()` singleton, so an open chat panel's own instance is the one erased, and BEFORE the record erase. Best-effort like the reminder hook: a failure goes to Sentry and never blocks the erase. Tests: `widget-src/src/storage/chat-history-store.test.ts` (4: tombstones all, merge with a pre-erase copy keeps the tombstones and the blank titles, a later `recordExchange` is refused, an empty history writes nothing), `packages/health-core/src/chat-history.test.ts` ("deleted is a monotonic tombstone and clears messages and the title"), `widget-src/src/lib/local-first-data.test.ts` (2: the erase tombstones history, and the record is erased even when the chat write fails).
- AC2b (2026-10-21, D4 decision D2): a conversation deleted, or every conversation erased, while a chat save is still in the air stays deleted on screen. The cloud save used to put its result in place of the working copy, so a save that started before the delete and answered after it brought the conversation back until a reload (the cloud file kept the tombstone). The save's result is now merged into the working copy (health-core `ChatSession`). The erase order moves into the record session with it (`RecordSession.deleteAllData`, O6): read the record, then the reminders teardown, then the chat tombstones, then the record erase, each step best-effort and reported. Tests: `chat-history-in-flight.test.ts` (failed first: a delete, and an erase, during an in-flight save), `chat-session.test.ts`, `record-session.session.test.ts` (the order, a failed step reported and the erase still made, neither step on a refused erase).
- AC3 (2026-09-10): a localStorage-only user's `health_roadmap_file_v2:chat-history.json` is removed by the erase. Only `LocalStorageAdapter.disconnect()` clears that prefix, and local mode skips disconnect (it would delete the erased record file itself), so the keys survived. The erase now sweeps the named-file prefix in local mode, which leaves the record file alone because its keys carry no colon. Order matters: the tombstone goes through the singleton FIRST, then the keys go — the other way round, a live store instance would conflict, re-read null, merge and resurrect. Test: `widget-src/src/storage/roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts`, "removes the named record files (chat history) but keeps the erased record file".
- AC3b: Completed local named-file cleanup invalidates stale local chat stores through a separate content-free generation marker that survives a later disconnect. A stale store's next ordinary read or write cannot restore the erased conversation; fresh chat remains possible. Chat does not parse unrelated roadmap JSON. The marker holds no conversation content, IDs, health values or timestamps and is not sent to cloud storage. A failed marker write reports incomplete cleanup as a warning, not a refusal: the record IS erased, so an erase answers `{success:true, warning:"Could not complete on-device history cleanup."}`, and the page still clears the chat's copy of the record (`health_roadmap_data`), mutes the embed, resets the form and shows the warning after the erase notice (AC8; Codex R2, adversary R1). Any failure after the erase's flush landed is a warning the same way; a refused erase (`ERASE_UNREACHABLE`, a failed flush) still answers `{success:false}` and rotates no marker. The chat and document keys are still gone (documents are removed before the marker is written). An answer that arrives after a local erase is not saved under a conversation the erase removed: each local chat store remembers, in memory only, the ids it held when it saw the marker change, and refuses them; a new conversation still saves (US-11 AC2, Codex R1). Known residual: the first answer of a conversation that held no saved exchange before the erase is saved, as on a cloud. Log-off is not stopped by it (US-09 AC2c). This does not make simultaneous localStorage operations transactional. Tests: `widget-src/src/storage/chat-history-local-erase.test.ts` (failed marker write in local and cloud mode; an answer landing after the erase in the erasing and a stale tab; a refused erase leaves the marker unchanged; independent stores over shared synthetic localStorage, not real multi-process browser proof), `widget-src/src/components/HealthTool.chat-profile.test.tsx` (the deletion flow with the mirror seeded and the marker write failing).
- AC4 (2026-09-10): an erase turns reminders OFF for anyone who had them on. Erasing an `active` opt-in left no `reminderOptIn` at all, which reads as "never decided", so the next storefront load auto-enrolled the user again through the address lane — refilling the server row the pre-erase hook had just torn down, with no token left in the widget to cancel it. The erased file now carries `reminderOptIn: { status: 'cancelled' }` whenever there WAS an opt-in, active or cancelled, and still carries no token or address. The manual toggle re-enrols, because that is the user asking. **What that re-enrolment then does, on the address lane (Dropbox, GitHub, typed):** it hits the existing US-17 AC8 path — the server refills the surviving row's schedule and returns no token, so the widget control keeps reading "Turn on" while the reminders send. Google Drive is unaffected: a Google-verified cancel deletes the row outright, so a Drive re-enrolment is a genuinely new one and gets its token. This is pre-existing behaviour for any existing row, not something the erase introduced; it is stated here because after an erase it becomes the normal path rather than the edge case. Tests: `widget-src/src/storage/roadmap-store-data-safety.test.ts` (2: an enrolled user comes out cancelled with no identity; a user who never decided still comes out with no record).
- AC5 (2026-09-10): the caveats are in the CONFIRM, not the alert afterwards. "This will permanently delete all your health data" was a promise the app cannot keep, and the things it cannot reach arrived after the click, too late to be a decision. The confirm now says what is erased (the health record and the chat history), then names the copies that stay: uploaded documents already in the cloud folder, connector import candidates (`imports/pending-*.json`) until the next import, the provider's version history and GitHub's past commits, and the command-line tool's backups beside the file, which stay only until that tool next writes the file (an erase write keeps no backup, and every later write prunes the copies that predate the erase epoch). It says reminders are turned off; that the row on our server keeps the address for 90 days so a later enrolment of that address does not send a second welcome email; that anyone who enrols the address again restarts the schedule, and each email carries the off link; and that cancelling from a Google sign-in deletes that row. **Corrected 2026-09-10 (second pass):** the sentence used to say the kept row means "a later re-enrolment does not restart them", which the code contradicts — `enrolByEmail` REFILLS a tombstone's schedule on the next optin (`app/lib/reminder-v2.server.ts`); the kept row only withholds the second welcome email. The post-erase alert says the same things, shorter, and has a second form for the erase whose chat-history write failed: `deleteUserData()` swallows that failure so an unreachable cloud cannot trap the user's data on their device, and now RETURNS `chatErased`, so the alert says the chat history could not be reached and is erased on the next chat (true: the tombstones sit in the `getChatHistory()` singleton and the next `recordExchange` merges them through `sync.save`) instead of claiming a deletion that did not happen. Tests: `widget-src/src/components/HealthTool.erase-copy.test.ts` (8, against the `ERASE_CONFIRM`/`ERASE_DONE`/`ERASE_DONE_CHAT_PENDING` constants that drive the dialogs — including that the confirm never claims the row stops reminders restarting), `widget-src/src/lib/local-first-data.test.ts` ("erases the record even when the chat-history write fails, and says so" asserts `chatErased: false`).
- AC6 (2026-09-24): an erase made on another device clears this device's drafts when this device takes it in, by a re-read or by a save: both drafts go by name, as in AC1, and since 2026-10-13 the Lp(a) check's kept answers too (Codex R2, adversary R7). Another tab of the same browser counts: its erase comes in by the re-read as it lands (US-34 AC6, 2026-09-25). Before, a draft typed here outlived the erase, and was committed into the new record when the user started again. A matrix on screen when the erase arrives drops its own copy too, with what it lent the plan and the chat (round 4: the other device erased and started again before this page re-read, so the matrix stayed on screen, wrote the draft back on the next keystroke and committed it into the new record on the next leave). Known gap: a page that was closed through the erase keeps no memory of the record it had, so a draft left on it is not cleared by its next load. Since 2026-10-21 (orchestrator O5, D4 step 5, corrected twice the same day after review) one clear serves both: an erase taken in from another device clears what AC1 clears here, stored document originals (`health_roadmap_doc_v2:*`) included, except the original of a document that outlives the erase. The record session decides which (`RecordSession.clearOffFileData`): a document live in the record after the erase (added after it, or never seen by it: US-09 AC20, AC23), or live in the device's own record copy (the localStorage record a guest or on-device fallback tab writes) once the erase is applied to that copy, keeps its original; an original the erase listed goes even where a stale device copy still names it, and a device copy that cannot be read names nothing. An erase made here goes by the same rule on the device tier, and the page's own clear after an erase (HealthTool) goes through it too: the page never clears stored originals itself. Residual: a cloud-tier erase made here still removes the device record and every stored original with it (the mirror wipe), so a row, a document's included, that a guest or fallback tab of this browser saves after the erase read the device record is lost with it, as before. - AC7 (2026-09-25; **an unreadable record now refuses the erase, and the time rule gave way to listed ids: US-09 AC23, 2026-10-20**): an erase beats the erase and fresh start of a copy it had not seen, and reports success only once it is written. `deleteUserData` bumped `eraseEpoch` from its own copy alone, so a tab or device that had not seen another's erase and fresh start erased at an EQUAL epoch; the merge unioned the two, the other copy's new rows stayed, and the erase reported success. It now bumps past the stored epoch too, read at erase time. The read is a round trip on a cloud, and a save could start during it: its flush then answered at once beside the running save, the erase reported success and wiped the device mirror, and a tab closed before that save's second pass lost the erase. Now a flush made while a save runs joins it and answers when that save ends, extra passes included: a later edit's failed pass can make the erase report a failure it did not have, never a success it did not have. A save ends before it announces anything, so a listener that saves again starts a new save. The erase also drops a change still on the debounce instead of saving it first, since the erase throws it away. That also closes the older window while the reminders cancel and the chat-history erase ran first. A failed erase counts as unsaved, so the next hide retries it (US-10 AC5). Residuals: a write that lands between the epoch read and the save's own read can still meet the erase at an equal epoch and union; an epoch read that fails leaves this copy's epoch, so the save can land beside a newer erase, merge instead of winning, and still report success; and an erase in an on-device fallback session bumps past the device file only, not the cloud it cannot reach. Since US-09 AC20 (2026-10-20) the erase beats the other copy's fresh start by time as well as epoch: that copy's measurements, lab values and documents created at or after the erase's `erasedAt` survive it, and that is a wall-clock comparison across two devices. The erase-time floor (`erasedAt` is 1 ms past the latest `updatedAt` the eraser read, its own included) means every row the eraser had seen goes whatever its clock says; a row written after the epoch read, or stamped by a clock running ahead, can still survive. Found by the Codex review of US-10 AC5 and the adversarial review after it. Tests: `roadmap-store-two-tabs.test.ts`, the US-11 AC7 block (a stale tab and a stale device erase over another's erase and fresh start; success only once the erase is written, with a save running when it began; no save of the change the erase throws away; a flush made by a listener to a save that just ended starts a new save; an erase that failed to save is written by the next hide).
- AC8 (2026-09-28, adversarial review): an erase empties the chat's copy of the record (`health_roadmap_data`, the copy the blog chat bubble and the chatbot embed read), and the embed on the page mutes.
