- AC40 (the plugin package is built and checked by one script — added 2026-10-02): `node docs/chatgpt-review/build-plugin-zip.mjs` builds the ZIP OpenAI takes from `docs/chatgpt-review/plugin/`; `--check` validates without writing. OpenAI publishes no validator, so the script encodes the documented rules and names each failure by its error code: the Agent Plugins `plugin.schema.json` and `mcp.schema.json` (no unknown keys), and OpenAI's submission errors with the stricter final-submission limits. It checks the plugin name's format and a semantic version; every text field's length and supported characters; HTTPS URLs that carry no credentials; a category from the published list; at most 20 capabilities; at most three starter prompts, unique and with no `@` mention; the logo and composer icon as a real PNG, square, 48 to 4096 px and at most 5 MiB; exactly five positive and three negative test cases, each positive case naming only tools in `MCP_TOOL_NAMES`; `commerce` a boolean; uppercase country codes; release notes; and exactly one `streamable-http` server over HTTPS. The folder may hold only `plugin.json`, `mcp.json` and nothing under `skills/`. A missing demo recording URL is a warning, not an error, because it can be set in the dashboard. The output is deterministic: entries sorted, every date fixed at 2026-01-01, so the same inputs give the same bytes; the script reads the archive back and fails unless it holds exactly the validated files, and refuses one over 100 MiB. Drift guards keep the hand-edited words in step with the server: the public guide describes every tool the server publishes and no other, and names the app as `plugin.json` does; the listing's annotation table matches each tool's declared hints; the package passes `--check`. - AC45 (2026-10-16): a client-metadata fetch refuses expanded mapped private addresses, 6to4, multicast, the `64:ff9b::/32` translation block outside the well-known NAT64 prefix (local-use `64:ff9b:1::/48` included), and IPv4-translated addresses (`0:0:0:0:ffff:0::/96`). An address in the well-known NAT64 prefix `64:ff9b::/96` (RFC 6052) is judged by the IPv4 address it carries, so a DNS64 answer for a public host passes: `64:ff9b::101:101` and `64:ff9b::1.1.1.1` (1.1.1.1) pass, while `64:ff9b::7f00:1` and `64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe` are refused, hex and dotted spellings alike (maintainer commit, 2026-10-19, plan option 2). A public address in the standard mapped prefix stays allowed, including the hex spelling `::ffff:0101:0101`, which the old remainder check refused. A public address written with a trailing dotted quad stays allowed. A string that starts with `fc` or `fd`, or with `::ffff:` but is not the mapped prefix, stays refused. An address the check cannot parse is refused. Teredo was not classified here; AC47 now refuses it with the rest of 2001::/23. Tests: ✅ `app/lib/mcp-auth.server.test.ts` ("rejects a non-public address written in another spelling", "judges a well-known NAT64 address by the IPv4 it carries").
- AC47 (2026-10-19, follow-up to AC45): a client-metadata fetch connects only to an address it checked. It uses Node's `https.request` with its own `lookup`: every address the name resolves to must be public or the connection fails, and the socket goes to an address from that same answer, so a DNS-rebinding resolver gets no second look. Node calls no lookup for an IP-literal host, so a literal is checked before any request, brackets stripped; a public literal is fetched as before. The fetch's agent keeps no TLS session (`maxCachedSessions: 0`) and no keep-alive, so a session ticket an attacker's server issued cannot ride a later connection to an internal address ("TLS poison"). What `fetch` did stays: one 5-second deadline over the whole request, body read included; every non-2xx refused, 3xx included, so no redirect is followed; a gzip, deflate or br body is decoded (`x-gzip` too), with the 64 KB cap checked on `content-length` and on the decoded bytes, so a decompression bomb is refused, and any other content encoding is refused; `application/json` required; no credentials, and a client id carrying userinfo is refused, because `node:https` would send it as an Authorization header; a port on fetch's bad-port list (the WHATWG list: 25, 6667, 10080 and the rest) is refused before any connection, and any other port is allowed, as before. The request carries `Accept: application/json`, `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br` and the user-agent `fetch` sent (`node`). It is not identical to fetch's: it drops fetch's `accept-language: *` and `sec-fetch-mode: cors`, and it asks to close the connection where fetch asked to keep it alive. The address check also refuses the reserved IPv4 blocks it let through (192.0.0.0/24, 192.0.2.0/24, 192.88.99.0/24, 198.18.0.0/15, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24; 240.0.0.0/4 was already refused), and an IPv6 address outside the IPv4 forms AC45 judges is public only in global unicast, 2000::/3, minus 2001::/23 (Teredo, which AC45 left unclassified, benchmarking, ORCHID), 2001:db8::/32, 2002::/16 and 3fff::/20. Pinned clients (Claude, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Codex) never reach this fetch. Usage signal: none new; the existing `unknown-client` refusal count. Tests: ✅ `app/lib/mcp-auth.server.test.ts` ("refuses the reserved ranges a public check must not pass", "refuses a client id that carries credentials, which node:https would send", "asks for JSON with a fixed user-agent, sends no credentials, and keeps no TLS session", "refuses a redirect, and every other answer that is not 2xx", "decodes gzip, deflate and br, as fetch did", "refuses a compressed body that decodes past the cap", "refuses a content encoding it does not decode", "refuses the ports fetch refused, and no other", "gives up after one 5-second deadline, whether the headers, the body or its decoding stall", "fetches a public IP-literal host as before", "passes a public answer through the connect-time lookup, in both shapes Node asks for"; on real sockets: "never opens a socket to an IP-literal host that is not public" for `https://127.0.0.1/`, `https://[::1]/` and `https://[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]/`, "connects only to the answer it checked, so a rebinding resolver gets no second look" (fails on the `fetch` version: the connection reached the loopback listener), "refuses a name whose answer mixes public and private addresses, before any socket opens", with happy-eyeballs on and off). ❌ Not tested: a real TLS handshake to a public host in CI. Checked by hand on 2026-10-19 from Brad's Mac: a scratch script removed the ChatGPT pin, so `https://chatgpt.com/oauth/client.json` took the fetch path, and it resolved to ChatGPT through the new path; the host answered brotli-encoded once the request sent `Accept-Encoding`.
- AC48 (a refusal says which branch fired — added 2026-10-20, follow-up to AC34): `mcp_authorize_refused` and `mcp_connect_failed` may carry a `detail`, one word from a closed list per reason (`MCP_OAUTH_DETAILS` in `packages/health-core/src/product-events.ts`), so the next refusal is diagnosable. Why: 14 refusal rows in 90 days, three of them organic (2026-10-03 `no-cookie`, 2026-10-07 `reviewer-credentials`, 2026-10-18 `unknown-client` from client `other`), and the row could not say which check fired. The words: `unknown-client` → `malformed` (neither our DCR id nor an https URL, or over 4096 characters), `dcr-invalid` (a DCR id that fails its HMAC or metadata), `cimd-refused-url` (userinfo, a refused port or a non-public IP literal, before any fetch), `cimd-fetch-failed` (no usable answer: unreachable, a host that resolves to a private address, a non-2xx status, a non-JSON content type, too large or too slow), `cimd-invalid` (a body that does not parse, or a `client_id` that is not the URL fetched), `cimd-redirect-refused` (redirects we do not allow); `redirect-uri` → `missing`, `unknown-host`, `known-host-other-path` and `loopback-other-path` (the same hostname as a registered redirect, differing in anything else; loopback when that registered redirect is a loopback one); `resource` → `other-host`, `other-path` (our host and port, but a different path or scheme; a non-default port is `other-host`); `no-cookie`, `token-dead-code`, `token-dead-refresh` → `missing` or `unseal-failed` (expired and tampered are one word: the seal cannot tell them apart cheaply). A detail is never a URL, host, client id, path, user agent, IP or any free text, and never a health value. The server allow-list keeps a detail only beside its own reason, on those two events; any other word, a detail with no reason, and a detail on any other event are dropped and the row kept. What the client is told does not change: same status, same body, same redirect, whatever the detail. Usage signal: the `detail` breakdown of the existing two counters. Tests: ✅ `app/routes/mcp.hosted.test.ts` ("a refusal names its branch in a closed word, and the answer does not change": each word emitted by its branch, every variant of a reason answered identically, reasons without a detail unchanged), `app/lib/mcp-auth.server.test.ts` ("a refused redirect names how it missed", a wrong scheme on a loopback host included), `app/lib/product-events.server.test.ts` ("keeps every closed detail word on its own OAuth reason", "drops a detail that is not a closed word, or not its reason's, and keeps the row", "keeps a valid reason and detail when an unrelated key is dropped").

Unset means `openai`: the box and sign-in behave exactly as under AC38, so deploying this shows no new box until Brad sets it (only the custody sentence's wording changes). The list gates the box and new sign-ins only; the kill switch is still the three secrets, and a reviewer session already connected outlives a change to the list. For those two it reads "Anthropic reviewers: sign in here" and "For Anthropic’s connector review only"; the ChatGPT and Codex box keeps its OpenAI wording. Everything else in AC38 is unchanged and shared: the same three secrets, username and password, the same failures-only limiter, the same reviewer record and shared connection bucket, the same kill switch. No variant of either id and no DCR client sees the box, whatever name or callback it claims (Claude falls back to DCR only if our metadata stops advertising CIMD and `none`; AC43's discovery keeps both). The custody sentence names both reviews ("while an OpenAI or Anthropic app review is pending"). One consequence, stated rather than hidden: the two vendors' reviewers share one account and one record, so unsetting or rotating a secret for one review ends the other's sessions too; the secrets come off only when neither review is pending, and between them the list goes back to the vendor still reviewing. ### US-33 · I follow the command-line guide and it works — **added 2026-09-02**
As someone comfortable in a terminal, or an AI coding agent working for me, I can open [guides/command-line.md](guides/command-line.md), run the commands in the order written, and get my plan and file a value — without reading the source of US-30 and US-31 to work out what they expect. US-30 and US-31 shipped the two commands; this is the walkthrough that makes them usable by someone who did not build them, and a sample record to practise on so nobody learns them against their own history.
- AC1 (it works end to end): every command in the guide runs against `docs/examples/health-roadmap.sample.json` in the order written and exits 0, except the one step the guide documents as a refusal: the occupied-day add exits 1 naming the row that holds the day, and the correction that follows appends a row keeping the original date and flips the old row to `entered-in-error`.
- AC2 (the guide cannot drift): `tools/walkthrough.test.ts` runs that sequence as real subprocesses and asserts the guide's `.md` still contains each command string it ran, so renaming a flag or a command fails CI instead of leaving a guide that tells the reader to type something that no longer exists.
- AC3 (the sample is a real record): `docs/examples/health-roadmap.sample.json` was built through the app's own code paths, not typed by hand, and it loads in the widget's data layer (`RoadmapStore.loadLatestMeasurements`) with its values current, and through `migrateFile` unchanged. It is fictional: no part of it came from a person.
- AC4 (honest first step): the guide states that no command creates a record — the app writes the file when a cloud provider is connected — and says where each backend keeps it, so a reader with no file is not left running commands that refuse.
- AC5 (2026-09-10, night): `get-plan --html` writes the report as private as the record it summarises. The file carries the same values, and `writeFileSync`'s mode is filtered by the umask, so on a permissive umask the plan landed world-readable in a shared directory. The write asks for `0600` and a `chmodSync` follows it, which also tightens a file that already existed. Tests: `tools/get-plan.test.ts`
- Usage signal (declared honestly, per the constitution): **none from us for the commands themselves, by design** — the same reason as US-29/30/31: they run on the user's machine against their own file. The guide is a published page, so the ONE thing that is countable is its traffic: page views and time on `/blogs/guides/command-line` in the existing site analytics, and GitHub traffic on the repo it sends people to. That measures whether anyone reads it, never whether anyone ran a command. If page views stay flat for a quarter, the guide is not the constraint and writing more of them will not help.
- Tests: ✅ `tools/walkthrough.test.ts` (3: AC1/AC2 the guide's eight commands run as real subprocesses in the order written, each asserted still present in the guide's `.md`, with the occupied-day refusal naming the row, the correction's append-and-flip read back off disk, and the `.bak` siblings pinned at 3; AC3 the sample through a real `RoadmapStore` and a `migrateFile` no-op). ❌ Not tested: `git clone` and `npm ci` (run by hand on a fresh clone, 2026-09-02, Node 22.19.0); the rendered HTML is built in CI's reach but read by eye.

### US-34 · The record on screen keeps up — **added 2026-09-02**
As someone with the roadmap open in a tab while my AI assistant edits my record — or with the same record open on my laptop and my phone — I see the change appear where I am looking, instead of wondering whether it worked and reloading the page to find out. US-32 made an assistant able to write; this is the half that makes a write visible to the person it was made for.
- AC1 (when it re-reads): `RoadmapStore.refreshFromRemote()` re-reads the record by the two steps of the ordinary `SyncManager.load()`, the adapter's `read` and the record's `migrate`, and merges what comes back with `mergeFiles` — no second read path, no second source of truth. A missing file is nothing to take in (AC6). It runs when the provider says the file moved, when the tab becomes visible, and when the window takes focus. **The provider's own change signal replaced the 60-second timer on 2026-09-02**: `StorageAdapter.watch(fileName, onChange, signal)` is optional, and an adapter that has one never runs the poll. Dropbox holds a `files/list_folder/longpoll` open against the app folder root (the `notify` host, which takes no access token — the cursor is the credential; `files/list_folder/continue` advances it before the store is told), so a write from another device or an assistant arrives in about a second, and a quiet tab costs two requests a minute. Google Drive has no browser long-poll — its push channels need a public webhook — so it walks `changes.list` from a `changes/startPageToken` every 3 seconds and calls only when a change names our file id: 20 requests a minute while the tab is visible, and none when it is not. Both back off on failure, doubling to a 60-second ceiling, and re-establish their cursor from scratch. A backend with no watch (GitHub and WebDAV have no cheap one) keeps the 60-second poll. localStorage's watch is the browser's `storage` event (AC6). A hidden tab watches and polls nothing — it has no screen to keep up to date, and a phone left on a background tab would spend the day holding a connection open; the watch is aborted when the tab is hidden and taken up again on return. A leading-edge 5-second throttle stops `focus` and `visibilitychange` — which fire together on a tab switch — making two round trips out of one return, and a push it swallows is held and re-read when the window is out: a watch fires once per change and then goes quiet, so dropping one would lose it. A return's own catch-up is held the same way, never dropped, and a hidden tab runs no re-read, a held one included (AC6).
- AC2 (a pending local edit always wins): it re-reads NOTHING while a save is in flight or the persist debounce is still pending, and it throws away a merge whose base moved while the read was in the air — the check after the read is that the working copy is the same OBJECT it merged from, because a save can start and finish inside the read window and leave `writePending` false again by the time the answer lands. The working copy is then AHEAD of the cloud, and merging a read taken before the edit existed would fight the write that is about to go up. The same rule holds on localStorage (AC6).
- AC3 (only a real change is announced): the merged file is compared to the working copy by CONTENT, with `meta` excluded — a merge always bumps the file's own clock, and Drive returns no version to compare, so bytes are the only honest test. Unchanged means no event, no re-render and no counted event. **Tightened 2026-09-24:** the ANNOUNCEMENT, from a re-read or from the change a save folds in, compares what a person would see: rows as a set and no record's own clock (`updatedAt`, `lamport`, and since US-10 AC6 `fieldStamps`). A merge re-sorts rows by id, and on an empty backend the first save trades the page's screenings stamp for the migration's; each was announced as a change, and the page reloaded over a weight being typed (2026-09-22, a guest on localStorage). Taking a merge IN still compares clocks: a skipped clock-only lead would leave the profile lamport behind the cloud's, and the next profile edit would lose the merge.
- AC4 (how the page hears): the store dispatches a DOM event, `hr:remote-changed` (`REMOTE_CHANGED_EVENT`, the same convention as `hr:sync-pending-changed`), and `HealthTool` re-runs the load path it already uses after an upload — `loadLatestMeasurements`, which carries the profile prefill. The store cannot call the API layer itself: the v2 builds alias `lib/api` to `lib/roadmap-data`, which imports the store, and the cycle would be real. The listener is registered once, in `initRoadmapStore`, which is where both surfaces start their data layer. **It does nothing while the demographics form is dirty** (`hasUnsavedProfileEdits`, over `PREFILL_FIELDS`): re-running the load path replaces the form's inputs, and a change landing on a half-entered height would take those keystrokes with it. Nothing is lost, and nothing waits on the user coming back: the change is HELD, and the save that carries the edit up replays it (`createRemoteChangeRelay`, `widget-src/src/lib/remote-replay.ts`) — several changes held during one edit collapse into a single re-render. The field the user is typing in rides through the re-render, and a field left with its save still waiting is saved first (2026-09-24): the load path replaces the demographics, never a weight half-typed. Nothing else in the form rides through. A first-time field's value gets none of a matrix draft's checks: it names the row it replaces only as it saves, not as it is typed (still open), and nothing stops it standing in once another writer fills its slot. Carried through a re-read, it would outrank that writer's value in the plan, then correct it. The field being typed in takes that risk, since losing keystrokes is worse; the journey redesign moves these fields onto the draft model. The matrices' drafts are not in the form (2026-09-25): what they lend the plan and the chat lives in its own state, so it rides through every re-read and is judged again against the record just read (US-03 AC6).
- AC5 (a bug this uncovered, fixed here): a profile-only edit in the app — changing sex, height or birth date with no measurement alongside it — called `applyProfileChanges` and never called `touch()`, so it scheduled no save at all and sat in memory until some later unrelated edit carried it up. Every other mutation on the store touches. Fixed in the same commit.
- AC6 (added 2026-09-25): another tab of the same browser is another writer. A guest's tabs share one on-device record, and a tab took in another tab's save only at its own next save (US-10 AC5). `LocalStorageAdapter.watch` now listens for the browser's `storage` event, which fires in every other tab of the origin when one tab writes a key. It calls for the record's key, and for a `clear()`, which names no key; the version key, other files and the drafts cost nothing. `refreshFromRemote` drops its local opt-out and keeps AC2's rule, so the re-read, merge, take-in (`adopt()`) and announcement are the cloud's own. Being watchable, the local tier runs no poll timer. A hidden tab drops any re-read the throttle was holding, and re-reads when shown; that catch-up waits out the throttle rather than being dropped, and the `focus` and `visibilitychange` that fire together still cost one read. The local tier's listener holds no connection, so it stays on while the tab is hidden (and from the start, for a tab opened hidden), and a save heard then reads nothing. The return (`visibilitychange` or `focus`) re-reads only when the stored revision, the record's version key, differs from the last one this tab took in (one `getItem`). The store holds that revision, and moves it only for what it merged in: its load, a re-read, and its own writes. A save's verify-after-write read never moves it, since it can see another tab's newer write that the save did not take in (Codex R1 on d19f4d8). A revision is a count plus a random suffix, so a record removed by a log-off and made again never repeats one a hidden tab has seen (Codex R2); only equality is asked of it, so an older bundle's plain count still checks. Residual, while tabs of mixed versions are open after a deploy: a bundle from before 94627c0 computes its next revision as `Number("4-abc") + 1`, which is NaN, so it writes "1" over any new revision, and a new tab hidden across two such writes can find "1" equal to "1" on return and show a stale record. Display only: every save still reads, merges and checks the version. It ends when the old tabs reload. Until the adversarial review of 2026-09-26 it re-read only if a `storage` event had been heard while hidden, and a page restored from the back-forward cache or an iOS tab the system suspended can miss that event, so it showed a stale record until its next write. So a lone guest tab never re-reads; until the 2026-09-25 cleanup it re-read and merged the whole record on every return and focus, and found nothing. Cloud tiers still drop the watch while hidden and re-read on every return. Before the Codex review's second round, a held re-read ran after the tab hid, moved the throttle on, and the return's catch-up was dropped, so a save made while the tab was hidden stayed unseen; that held on every backend. A burst of saves in the other tab, a lab import say, costs at most one re-read every 5 seconds, not one per save: the throttle reads the first at once and holds the rest for a trailing re-read. Another tab's erase comes in by the same take-in, so it clears this tab's drafts (US-11 AC6). A re-read never writes, and a missing file, on any backend, is nothing to take in: the empty record `migrate` makes for one holds no field, and an object with none never wins the merge (US-10 AC6), so the re-read is `SyncManager.load()` again and the merge changes nothing. Before that rule its fresh stamps beat this tab's profile and screenings wherever their lamport was 0 or absent (a record written by hand or by an older app; found by the Codex review of this AC), and the re-read had to tell a missing file apart itself. So a record another tab removed (a log-off, or a cloud erase wiping the device copy) brings nothing in: this tab keeps what it shows and any edit it has not saved, and puts nothing back. Following the removal instead would suit a log-off, but it would destroy rows this tab saved since the other tab last lifted the record, which may exist nowhere else; a file made again can be erased again, a dropped copy is gone. Its next save does make the device file again from its own copy (US-10 AC5's residual). That save merges the missing file as the empty record, which since US-10 AC6's empty-object rule leaves a profile or screenings with no lamport as it was; before, it emptied them. Residuals: the event's propagation, the throttle and a pending edit here each delay a take-in. The usage signal below counts these take-ins too: `HealthTool` fires `remote_change_applied` for every announced change, whatever wrote it. So since this AC a count no longer shows by itself that an assistant or a second device is at work; a guest's second tab counts as well, and since 2026-09-26 `backend: local` tells it apart. A cloud count still does not tell another cloud tab, a second device or an assistant apart. And one burst of saves in the other tab, a lab import say, can count twice: the throttle's leading re-read and its trailing one each announce.
- Usage signal (declared, per the constitution): `remote_change_applied` in `product_events` — fired by `HealthTool` when it has actually re-rendered on a remote change. Its one metadata key, since 2026-09-26, is `backend`: `local` (another guest tab of this browser) or `cloud` (the record lives in a cloud; the change came from another tab, another device or an assistant), a closed list the server's schema enforces. Only guest tabs split out: `cloud` does not tell another cloud tab from another device or an assistant. Never which field changed, never a value. Read against `results_viewed`: if it stays at zero once the connector guides are out, either nobody is running an assistant against a record they also have open, or the re-read is not firing — and the two are told apart by whether hosted MCP tool calls are happening at all.

### US-35 · My assistant imports my lab files — **built 2026-09-04, verified live 2026-09-05 (hosted API on the scratch Dropbox: commit, replay, conflicts, 90-day rule, documents; ChatGPT drag + folder routes on Brad's record, extract only; Drive refusal)**
As someone who keeps a ZIP of lab PDFs and clinic letters (Brad's own is `health.zip`), I can drop the file into my connected Dropbox folder and say "import it", or drag it into ChatGPT and say the same, and my assistant reads every document, shows me what it found against what my record already holds, and files only what I confirm — instead of retyping thirty numbers or leaving the chat for the website. The website's upload already does extraction, review and a bulk save (lab-upload.md); this is the same pipeline reached through the connector, with the review step done in words. Design brief and the resolved decisions from its adversarial review: [mcp-import-design.md](mcp-import-design.md). Architecture context: [mcp-architecture.md](mcp-architecture.md) §3, §7.
- AC1 (one tool, two phases, and the first never writes): a single tool `import_documents` in `packages/health-core/src/mcp-tools.ts`, published on every surface like the other seven. Called with a source (AC2, AC4) it EXTRACTS and returns candidates plus a `receipt`; called with `commit` (AC8) it WRITES; `commit` beside a source is refused. An extract call opens the record read-only and saves nothing, ever — a test asserts the record's version is unchanged after an extract that found values. The server keeps nothing between the two phases: the candidate payload is parked in the USER's own folder (AC7).
- AC2 (the folder route, Dropbox): with no `file` argument the tool lists the ROOT of the connected app folder (`dropboxListFolder`, files only, `has_more` followed) and takes the files named in `fileNames`, or every importable file when the argument is absent. Importable is `.pdf`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.png`, `.zip` by the shared `isImportableEntryName` rule; `health-roadmap.json`, folders, dotfiles and everything else are ignored, not refused. A name in `fileNames` is matched by equality against the listing and the file is downloaded by the listing's `id`, so a name never forms a path; a name not in the listing refuses the call and names what the folder holds. The file is `{v: 2, payload, issued, mac}`: `issued` in epoch seconds, and `mac` 32 lowercase hex characters (128 bits) of HMAC-SHA256 under an HKDF key from `MCP_SEAL_KEYS` with info `mcp/import-step/v1`, distinct from every blob type's. The MAC covers the kind, the id, `issued`, the payload's sha256, the connection hash, and the client and resource hashes. It is signed with the first key and checked against every configured key, so a rotation inside the hour does not strand a receipt; a key since removed opens nothing. Commit checks, in this order and BEFORE anything is charged, so a forged or foreign receipt costs nothing and deletes nothing: the UUID shape (else not valid); the pending file (missing: "That receipt names no pending import: it was committed, discarded or mistyped. Nothing was written. Extract again if the user still wants it."); its shape, `v` 2 (else not readable); the MAC for this connection and client, compared with `timingSafeEqual` (else not valid for this connection); the one-hour window, with an `issued` up to 60 s ahead of our clock taken as skew and more refused as not valid (else expired). Nothing in it was secret, and in the 1.0.2 demo run ChatGPT's approval card called it an "opaque or disguised payload" and once blocked the commit. A commit deletes the file it consumed at once, best effort: a delete that fails is one Sentry count carrying no file name, no path and no error text, and what it costs is a file that outlives its use, not a leak of anything the user did not already own. There is no discard action — an import the user declines is simply never committed, and its file is swept. The sweep is the backstop, not the cleanup: it takes `imports/pending-*.json` files older than twice a receipt's life (two hours, past which nothing can still be committed from one), never another file the user keeps in that folder. Two changes on 2026-09-10, from the adversarial review: the window was 24 h, and the sweep ran only inside `extract` — which `file_results` and every Google Drive user never call, so their abandoned pending files were never swept at all. It now runs in `stash`, the one door every route passes through, so the next import of any kind clears the last one's residue. A payload the model retyped is exactly `add_lab_values`, which exists. **Changed 2026-10-07 (later):** a commit also carries `approval`, the user’s own words approving these candidates, quoted from their message (1 to 200 characters). Privacy: the words live in memory for one request and are never stored, logged, hashed, counted or echoed back. The stdio server accepts the field and ignores it. - AC17 (2026-10-19, PR #163): The shared bulk writer validates each core measurement's metric name, finite numeric value and existing plausibility bounds before touching its slot or correction target. Typed `measurementRefusals` identify invalid core rows separately from duplicates and lab-unit refusals; an invalid correction cannot supersede a valid row or claim the slot against a later valid input. A refusal's message names the reason, never the value, as `LabUnitRefusal`'s does; an out-of-range refusal also carries `bound` (`above` or `below`), which end of the range it missed. The website shows each refusal the way it shows a refused lab unit: a settled outcome, not a save error, so the done screen names the test once on its own line and offers no retry (US-12 AC6). The line says what is out of range: the test's name and the end of the range it missed, in the unit the person reads (Lp(a) in its field's own unit: nmol/L, mg/dL or mg/L), never the value. That end is the SI bound the record enforced, converted and rounded inward, so the value is always past the number shown: LDL's 12.9 mmol/L reads "above 498 mg/dL", since 499 mg/dL is refused; the form's US-unit messages round the same way ("at most 498 mg/dL", "at least 45 lbs") (Brad, 2026-10-20: "explain what's out of range, otherwise it will confuse users"): "PSA not saved: above 10,000 ng/mL, the highest value this tool accepts. Check the report, then enter it again.", or "below 9 mmol/mol, the lowest value…" for a floor. A connector commit containing a refused core row is rejected as a whole before any selected values or documents are written. Lab conversion and receipt semantics are unchanged. One clinical bound moved (Brad, 2026-10-19, raised again 2026-10-20): the PSA ceiling is 10,000 ng/mL, up from 100, because metastatic prostate cancer can read in the hundreds or thousands. It holds on the form and the upload alike. `evidence.ts` and `roadmap_text.html` state no PSA maximum, so they do not change. The triglycerides, LDL and Lp(a) ceilings stay. Usage signal: `measurement_refused`, sent by the browser once per tab for each metric and reason, with metadata `{ refusal }`, one of `MEASUREMENT_REFUSAL_REASONS` (`unknown-metric`, `invalid-value`, `out-of-range`), plus `metric`, a `METRIC_TYPES` id, for `invalid-value` only (`MEASUREMENT_REFUSALS_WITH_METRIC`). An `unknown-metric` name is free text; an `out-of-range` metric would tell analytics this visitor's value for that test is past a clinical bound (Brad, 2026-10-20), and the server refuses that row. The browser still counts one event per tab for each (metric, refusal) pair: an out-of-range metric keys the tab's throttle locally and is never sent. Never the value. It is not `lab_unit_refused`, whose rows list spellings to teach the catalogue. ### US-36 · My assistant reads my files and my record stays structured — **built 2026-09-07 (Brad approved assistant-side extraction as the default for files in the chat; the 2026-09-07 design review's three blockers are folded into AC2/AC4, AC9 and AC10 below; live verification pending)**
As someone who drops a lab PDF, a photo of a result sheet or a clinic letter into ChatGPT or Claude and says "add this", my own assistant reads the file with its own eyes and sends our server only what it read — a metric, the name as printed, the number, the unit as printed, the collection date — and our server checks every row against the catalogue, the unit tables and the plausibility ranges, slots it against my record, and files only what I confirm. No file byte and no extraction spend touch Brad's server on this route. The honest sentence, everywhere it is said: the file never reaches our server; only the values my assistant read do, in memory for one request, and they are written to my own folder, never kept by us. The website's upload and the Dropbox folder route (US-35) are unchanged. Evidence for the decision: on 13 synthetic and 6 real NZ reports a Sonnet-class assistant matched our Haiku pipeline on every value and caught the one real misread it made (Lp(a) filed as ApoB); a Haiku-class assistant matched the numbers and asked for a missing date instead of guessing; the same small model followed a planted instruction in a clinic letter 5/6 times and called `correct_value`, which is why AC9 exists. Not approved, not built: a server-side watcher or webhook.
- AC1 (one new tool, not a widened old one): `file_results` in `packages/health-core/src/mcp-tools.ts`, listed on every surface beside the eight. `add_lab_values` keeps its shape and meaning exactly (it is in the listed ChatGPT app 1.0.0, the stdio server and the CLI, and a typed panel needs no receipt); `import_documents` keeps its folder route. `file_results` takes ONE file per call: `sourceFileName`, `classification` (`lab_report` | a `DOCUMENT_TYPES` value), `collectedOn` (YYYY-MM-DD, required — a file with no printed date is the assistant's to ask the user about, never to guess), `values[]` (≤`MAX_LAB_ROWS_PER_CALL`, each `metric` (a core key or a lab catalogue key or the printed name), `printedName` as printed, `value`, `unit` as printed, optional `referenceLow`/`referenceHigh`, optional `recordedAt` overriding the file's date) and an optional `document` block (`title`, `date`, `type`, optional `summary` ≤120 chars, optional `sha256` of the bytes when the client can compute it). `commit` is the same block `import_documents` takes and is refused beside a source. The stdio server lists it and runs it too — it needs no model and no network, so unlike `import_documents` it is not hosted-only; there the receipt is the payload id, and the payload lives in the server process's memory (a restart loses it: extract again), because `FileAdapter` serves one file and cannot park a pending one beside it. A `clinic_letter` or other non-lab call with neither `values` nor `document` is refused: a letter is filed from its `document` block, never from a bare file name.
- AC2 (the server checks, never trusts): every row runs the same dry run `prepareImport` runs today (`appendMeasurement` on the value already converted to canonical by AC4, `appendLabValue` with the lab's own unit (superseded 2026-09-18: a catalogued lab test is stored in its SI unit, US-21 phase 3; an uncatalogued one still keeps the unit it was reported in)) — a core metric outside `healthInputSchema`'s range, a day that has not happened, a core metric under a lab name — is refused row by row, never the call, and each refusal is one line in `unrecognized` naming the row, the reason and the way round it ("ldl 320 mmol/L is outside 0.5–15 mmol/L (20–580 mg/dL): check the unit; if the report really says that, tell the user and do not file it"). A result printed as a bound ("<0.5", ">90") is not a number and the description says to report it, not file it. Honest limit: the dry run cannot catch a unit swap on a metric whose floor is 0 — `ldl`, `total_cholesterol`, `hdl`, `triglycerides`, `apob`, `lpa` (`healthInputSchema` is `min(0)` there; only HbA1c and creatinine have a physiological floor) — so an SI number sent under the conventional label (LDL 3.4 "mg/dL" → 0.09 mmol/L) passes the range; AC4's display-floor check is what catches it, as a question, not a refusal. No range changes (three-file sync untouched). A per-value `recordedAt` that is not on the calendar ("2026-02-30", which `Date` rolls to 2 March) is refused the same way, as one line, by the one `isCalendarDay` check in `measurement-history.ts` that `resolveRecordedAt`, the extraction parse (US-12 AC12) and the reminder schedule share (2026-10-18). Test: `mcp-tools.test.ts` "refuses a per-value day that is not on the calendar".
- AC3 (the name check — the misread this design exists for): the server resolves `printedName` to a key — core metrics through a `CORE_METRIC_ALIASES` table lifted from `UNIFIED_SYSTEM_PROMPT`'s alias list into code (the prompt is then generated from the table, so one list), lab tests through `resolveLabCatalogEntry` — and REFUSES a row whose printed name resolves to a different key than `metric` claims ("Lipoprotein(a)" cannot be filed as `apob`; the line says "printed name Lipoprotein(a) is lpa, not apob — re-send it as lpa"). A core `metric` whose printed name resolves to nothing is refused too, with "if the report really calls ldl that, tell the user and add it with add_measurement"; a lab `metric` whose printed name resolves to nothing is filed under `labSlotKey(printedName)`, as an uncatalogued test is today. The match is EXACT after folding (case, whitespace), never a substring: "Cholesterol" alone (the NZ/UK print) is `total_cholesterol`, "LDL Cholesterol (calc)" is `ldl`, "HDL Cholesterol" is `hdl`, while "Non-HDL Cholesterol", "Chol/HDL ratio" and "Total/HDL ratio" resolve to nothing and are pinned as non-matches. A `printedName` that is the bare core key the assistant sent as `metric` ("apob"/"apob") is refused as lazy: it is not a name a report prints, and it would make the check pass without a check. Honest limit: the check is only as good as `printedName`; it catches the honest misread (the model printed the real name and mis-keyed it), not a dishonest one. The candidate the user confirms shows `printedName` beside the metric, so "Lipoprotein(a) → lpa" is what they read.
- AC4 (units): a core-metric row's `unit` must match one of the metric's known labels — `lookupUnit` over `UNIT_ALIASES` in `units.ts`, the ONE table, which `reportedToCanonical` (add_measurement, correct_value) and the chatbot's edits now consult too, aliases included (`umol/L`, `micromol/L`, `%`, `mg/dl`, and the scaled ones below), never the range-guessing fallback — and is converted to canonical; an unknown unit is refused with the two labels named ("hba1c is measured in mmol/mol or %, not "g/dL""). Two scaled aliases: Lp(a) `mg/L`, the NZ/AU/UK print (×0.1 to mg/dL, the conventional label since 2026-10-13, then ×2.5 nmol/L per mg/dL, 2.4 until 2026-10-13; the factor is per mg/dL, NOT per mg/L — corrected 2026-09-07 after 45 mg/dL was refused as 1080 nmol/L; see US-05 AC1) and ApoB `mg/L` (÷1000 to g/L); the candidate keeps the printed value and unit beside the converted one, because the Lp(a) mass→molar factor is an average. Wrong-direction guard: a core value whose canonical form falls below the metric's display floor (`UNIT_SWAP_FLOORS`: lipids 0.3 mmol/L, ApoB 0.1 g/L, Lp(a) 0.5 nmol/L = 0.2 mg/dL; a band stated once beside `UNIT_ALIASES`, not a range change) is offered with `confidence: 'low'` and a `question` ("3.4 mg/dL is 0.09 mmol/L; was the printed unit mmol/L?") rather than `high`. A lab row keeps the unit as printed (the record's own rule, agent-access rule 8); a catalogue `unitAlias` relabels it. Candidates display in the record's `profile.unitSystem`, as `import_documents` does.
- AC5 (slots, dedup, confirm — identical to US-35): rows are slotted by `prepareImport` against a fresh read of the record: `free`, `held_equal` (nothing written), `held_different` with `replaceable` under the 90-day rule; additional-lab equality uses the value-and-unit comparison in US-35 AC6, not bare reported numbers; two rows for one (metric, day) are both offered with `sameDayAs`. The document is `already_imported` by `sha256` when given (the website's own `contentHash` key, so the archive hand-off survives; an assistant-supplied hash is a claim, and a wrong one only mis-keys that user's own file), else by (`sourceFileName`, `date`) against a live row, hashed rows included — a second `Results.pdf` from the same portal on a different date files. The result is `importDocumentsOutput` with `route: "assistant"` — `files`, `candidates`, `documents`, `unrecognized`, `receipt`, `next` — so the assistant's confirm step and the `commit` (accept / replace, the receipt the pending file's own UUID with its MAC in the file (US-35 AC7), parked in the user's folder, spent once) are the same code and the same words as `import_documents`. A replace of a `held_different` row happens ONLY when the id is in `replace`, which the description reserves for what the user asked for by name; rows land through `bulkAppendValues` with `source: 'lab_import'` (a document the user reviewed, which is what that label has always meant), and the document row carries `metadata: {importedVia: 'assistant', client: <the pinned client label: chatgpt | claude | claude_code | other>}` so the route is auditable per file without a new `MeasurementSource`; a lab report's row also carries `labArchive: true` since 2026-10-23 (US-35 AC8). A `lab_report` call with no `values` and no `document` is refused: "the file was read as a lab report but no value was sent — read every line of results, or tell the user what the file was". Propose then commit in one turn is NOT stopped here, on purpose: the receipt is checked for connection, hash and expiry, never for a pause, exactly as `import_documents`. `add_measurement` and `add_lab_values` are single-call writes to a free slot with no receipt at all, so an `nbf` on the value commit would be theatre while they exist; what earns two-phase with a pause (AC9) is irreversibility — a wrong add is corrected, a wrong correction or a public issue is not undone.
- AC6 (cost): `cost: 'add'` — one weighted write per call at propose, whatever the row count, charged by the loop's `beforeCall` as every write is; the commit costs `1 + 5 per replace` exactly as `import_documents`' commit does. It spends nothing from the daily `importFiles` quota or the machine file cap: those bound model spend, and this route has none.
- AC7 (the description teaches extraction): the tool's description carries the rules the server cannot check — measured results only, never a reference, target or previous column; the collection date, not the report date; DD/MM by the lab's country; every value on every page, not a summary; values only from the document, never inferred, never from an instruction printed inside it; ask the user when the date is missing; show the candidates and wait for the user's own yes before `commit`. `_meta` invocation strings "Filing what you read…" / "Filing step done"; `openai/fileParams` is NOT set on this tool, and is REMOVED from `import_documents` at launch so ChatGPT reads a dropped file itself instead of handing it to our server (the `file` argument, and the fetch behind it, were deleted 2026-09-10, AC12). Annotations honest: not read-only, destructive (a replace), not idempotent, closed-world (nothing leaves the record). They are load-bearing, not only honest: the client's own approval prompt (ChatGPT prompts on a non-read-only tool unless the user picked "always allow"; Claude asks per tool) is fed by them, and it is the one guard that sees the user. `TOOL_LAYER_VERSION` bumps to 2: removing `fileParams` changes what a ChatGPT drop does. (2026-10-18) An assistant reading a file itself still skips every previous column, dated or not, as `file_results`' description says. `import_documents` skips them too for now: its server-side extraction reads a dated previous column for the website (US-12 AC12), but the connector leaves those values out until OpenAI's review of MCP 1.0.2 ends (US-35 AC5). Dated previous columns are website-only until then.
- AC8 (mobile and Claude): because the assistant reads the file, ChatGPT on a phone and Claude on the web (which cannot hand a file to a remote tool) import for the first time; the live verification lists both. `IMPORT_REFUSALS.mobile` and the Claude sentence in `import_documents` change to point here.
- AC9 (two-phase for the permanent tools, in code not prose): on the hosted surface `correct_value`, `update_profile` and `report_feedback` become propose-then-confirm. A call without `confirm` runs every existing guard (`expectedValue`, `expected`, the 90-day rule, the health-value scan), charges its full cost, writes NOTHING, and answers with what it would do and a `confirm` receipt — UUID-shaped, `iiiiiiii-jjjj-mmmm-mmmm-mmmmmmmmmmmm` in lowercase hex: `i` the issue time in epoch seconds (32 bits, good until 2106), `j` 16 random bits, `m` 80 bits of HMAC-SHA256 under the `mcp/proposal-step/v1` HKDF key over the kind, the issue time, `i` and `j` exactly as received, the call's identity (the tool and its canonical arguments), the connection hash, and the client and resource hashes. Anything that is not exactly that shape (uppercase, padding, whitespace, another length) is refused before any other check. It is not valid before 10 s after issue (an issue time up to 60 s ahead of our clock is skew and counts as early; further ahead is not ours) and expires at 15 min, both read from one window table (`STEP_WINDOWS`) at issue and at verify; signed with the first seal key, checked against all; `next` says "show this to the user and call again with `confirm` after their own yes". The same call with `confirm` set, the same arguments (hash-checked) and the same connection then writes, uncharged. A receipt used early, twice, on other arguments or on another connection is refused in words. Other arguments, another tool, another connection or client, and a receipt that is not ours get ONE refusal, because the MAC covers them all: "That confirm receipt does not match these arguments on this connection, or is not ours. Nothing was written. Call <tool> again without confirm, with exactly what the user approved, to propose afresh." Expired and early keep their own words. Nothing is charged and nothing is thrown before the receipt verifies. The stdio server ignores `confirm` (a person is watching their own file, as with `expectedValue`). For `report_feedback` the hash is over the PREPARED text (`title` one-lined, `detail` printable, whitespace collapsed, case folded), so a re-emitted report that drifts in spacing still confirms; the refusal for an early confirm names the moment the receipt becomes valid and says "do not retry before then; end your turn". Single-use is per machine, keyed on the whole receipt plus the connection hash (the `spentCodes` pattern, best-effort across Fly machines; a replay on a second machine meets `not-active` on `correct_value`, an `expected` mismatch on `update_profile`, and could file a second public issue). **Accepted residual, stated 2026-09-10:** `spentProposals` is per machine and both Fly apps run two machines during a canary deploy, so a receipt replayed inside its 15 minutes can file a second public issue. Accepted rather than closed: the replay needs the receipt the user's own assistant holds, and a stateless close would cost a GitHub search per filing. No code. What the server enforces, exactly: a permanent write takes two calls, identical arguments, the same connection, at least 10 s apart and within 15 min. What it does not: an assistant with a code tool can sleep 10 s; five reads in a row take as long; a receipt held into the next turn is still valid. What two-phase buys for real: the proposal lands in the transcript before the write, where the user can read it and interrupt, the client's approval prompt runs twice, and an injected model must emit a second call carrying the receipt, which the review's 5/6 measurement never tested. Status: the two-phase flow against a Haiku-tier assistant is UNTESTED until the live verification runs it; the claim that AC9 closes the 5/6 case waits on that. In CI: a deterministic scripted assistant replays the planted sequence (propose writes nothing and charges; confirm at +2 s, with altered arguments, replayed, and from another connection all refused; confirm after `nbf` writes once, uncharged), and the three injection PDFs run against a real model only under `CONNECTOR_SMOKE=1` (a monitor, not a regression test; monthly by the `connector-smoke` registry row). **Changed 2026-10-07:** the receipt was a ~400-character sealed `'proposal'` blob, and in the 1.0.2 demo run ChatGPT blocked the `correct_value` confirm that carried one. It is now UUID-shaped, like the row ids that passed unflagged. The separate "different arguments" and "not valid for this connection" refusals became the one above. Usage signal: every two-phase `mcp_tool_call` row carries `step: propose|confirm` (server-only, closed, owned by that event), so the confirm rate is confirm rows over propose rows per tool; a proposal with no confirm is a write the user declined or the client blocked, which is how the 2026-10-07 block would now show. **Changed 2026-10-07 (later):** the confirming call also carries `approval`: the user’s own words approving the change, quoted from their latest message, 1 to 200 characters. Later that day, on the reviewer record, the user typed "Yes, correct it." and pressed Allow once, and ChatGPT's safety layer still blocked the `correct_value` confirm twice; no confirm reached the server (product_events show only `step: propose`). Its approval card said: "the call includes a confirmation receipt but no evidence of the user's own-word approval". The tool text allows the second call only after the user's own yes, in their own words, and ChatGPT's monitor judges the call, not the chat, so the call now carries that evidence. The rule: a call with `confirm` and no `approval`, or a blank one, is refused after the receipt's shape, MAC and window are checked (so a chained call at +2 s still gets the early refusal, "end your turn") and before the receipt is claimed, so it costs nothing and spends nothing (adversarial review R1): "If the user has not yet answered the proposal in their own words, show it to them and end your turn. Otherwise quote the user’s approval: call <tool> again with the same arguments, confirm set to the same receipt, and approval set to the user’s own words approving this change, quoted from their message. Nothing was written." One over 200 characters is refused too, in its own words. `approval` is stripped with `confirm` before the tool runs, so it is not part of the call's identity: different words still confirm the same proposal. The server cannot tell whether the words are really the user's; what it adds is the evidence ChatGPT's monitor asked for, in the call it judges. Privacy: the words live in memory for one request and are never stored, logged, hashed, counted or echoed back. The stdio server accepts the field and ignores it. A refused confirm counts as `outcome: refused, reason: confirm, step: confirm`. Tests: `app/routes/mcp.hosted-guards.test.ts` (refused without words, uncharged, the receipt still good; a chained confirm without words told to wait; blank, non-text and 201 characters refused; other words confirm the same proposal; the words never reach any file), `app/routes/mcp.hosted.test.ts` (no words in any counter row), `packages/health-core/src/mcp-tools.test.ts`, `tools/mcp-server.test.ts`.

Only the values it read do, in memory for one request, and they are written to your own folder, never kept by us" (never "nothing passes through our server": the values do); the folder route keeps its sentence ("read by our server and sent to Anthropic for extraction, not kept"). The consent page's Google Drive paragraph changes too: with `file_results` the chat route works on Drive, on a phone and on Claude.
